Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 1:

﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾

These (letters) also occur in other surahs: in Surat al-'Ankabut, Surat al-Rum, Luqman and al-Sajda. Some surahs add a ra' to them, and some add a sad, as in "Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad" and "Alif. Lam. Mim. Ra'." All of this comes either as emphasis of the meanings or as emphasis of the secret (sirr) that God placed in these letters, even though we do not grasp that secret.

A person benefits from the secrets of things that the One who originated things has placed in them, even if he does not know those secrets; he is still benefiting from them. Let us give an example: the villager who has no knowledge of electricity, does he benefit from electricity or not? He benefits from it. He presses the switch of the lamp to light it or to extinguish it. Does he know the secret of that? No. Yet he has benefited from it. Likewise the believer, when he says "Alif. Lam. Mim," takes its secret from the one who uttered it, whether he understands it or does not. So the matter does not need us to philosophize about it. It is true that the human intellect circles around a thing in order to become familiar with it, but the giving of God and the wisdom of giving lie above what we can become familiar with and above what we find strange.

As for the word of the Truth, glorified is He, at the end of Surat al-Baqara: ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people﴾, it also suits Surat Al 'Imran. Why? Because Islam was coming to confront the camp of disbelief and the camp of the People of the Book. So that the call of God, which came from God through the procession of all the messengers who preceded Muhammad (ﷺ), should not be split apart, and so that it would not seem that this (message) came to contradict some part of it, it came to strengthen the call of God, and so that the nations that followed these religions would be in the ranks of Islam. Therefore, when the Arabs denied the message of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God said to them: ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾, meaning that whoever has knowledge of the Book bears witness that you are the Messenger of God.

﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is God as witness between me and you, and (so is) whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

It was expected of the People of the Book that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came, they would be the first to believe in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because he came to affirm the procession of faith, and he brings them a surah named Al 'Imran so that everyone knows that you, O Muhammad, did not come to demolish the religion of 'Isa, but to preserve the religion of 'Isa and to support it. So if you who believed in 'Isa are believers in 'Isa, then hasten immediately to belief in Muhammad. God named it Al 'Imran and made for them a surah in the Qur'an.

The message of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not come out of tribalism, nor to erase what came before it, as human tribalisms do when one people comes upon the ruins of another and demolishes everything connected to those people, even erasing their history and disfiguring their things, because they want to create a new history. No, this Qur'an wants to correct history. It brings a surah called "Al 'Imran," and that is a lofty honour for this religion and for its followers.

After that the Truth comes and opens it with His saying, exalted is His majesty: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾.

**Allah! There is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting (al-Hayy al-Qayyum).**

That is the central issue, which is why the Qur'an repeats this affirmation: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him﴾. In grammatical terms, ﴿Allah﴾ is the *mubtada'* (subject of the nominal sentence), and ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is the *khabar* (predicate). The subject must be clear in the mind, so the word ﴿Allah﴾ is already clear in the mind. But He wants to give the word ﴿Allah﴾ the description that befits Him, which is ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. For this reason the Truth says:

﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they deluded?﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:61].

So Allah is clear in their minds. But the temporal authorities wanted to obscure this clarity, so the Qur'an came to remove and erase this obscuring, affirming ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him﴾. This is a matter that the Truth declared as His own testimony about Himself:

﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:18].

"And sufficient is Allah as a witness" (4:79), because it is the testimony of the Essence to the Essence. The angels testified by witnessing, for they saw no one else but Him. Likewise, those of knowledge testified, those who draw from the evidences in the universe what confirms the truth of the angels and affirms the truth of Allah. If we look at it from another angle, we say: the Truth declared it about Himself and said, ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. He made it the word of tawhid (monotheism) and made the matter extremely easy, simple and straightforward. Allah did not will that the proof of belief in a Supreme Power be a complicated proof, or a philosophical proof, or one that no one can reach except people of high culture. No, religion is a demand for everyone, from the shepherd to the philosopher. It is required of the one who sweeps the street just as it is required of the university professor.

Therefore the question of faith must be at the level of all these minds. There is no philosophy in this matter. For this reason the Truth willed to make this matter utterly simple, and Allah made it clear: "I testify that there is no god but I." Then either the matter is true, and the problem ends and no one has the right to object; or it is not true, and then tell us: where is the other god who heard the challenge, and whom Allah stripped of that universe, saying, "I am alone in the universe, and I am the One who created"? Then we heard no reply from him, nor any opponent to him. Did that other god not realize?

So that other one cannot be a god. If that other one knew this and did not defend himself or his ownership of the universe, then he is not fit to be a god. The matter stands in Allah's favour until some claimant appears to contest it. So ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is a word of truth, and by reason and logic He is God, and we have found no opponent. We said earlier that a claim, when it is made and no opponent is found when we hear it, belongs to its owner until an opponent appears. We gave an example: we were gathered in a room, ten people, and after they left the owner of the house found a wallet. Then one man came, anxious, and said: "I have lost my wallet."

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾

The owner of the house said to him: "We found a wallet, but there were ten people here." When the ten were brought and questioned, no one claimed it. So it belongs to him.

Allah has said ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. If there were another god, let him appear to us. But only the power of Allah appears to us, ﴿there is no god but Him﴾. And since there is no god but Him, and this universe needs a Self-Subsisting One to manage it, He must be Living with a life that befits Him. For He grants many lives to all kinds of creatures: to humans, to animals, to plants and to inanimate things. Therefore the One who brings these into existence must be living, and His life must be suited to Him.

The word "Qayyum" is called by them an intensive form (*sigha mubalagha*), because when an action occurs, it occurs sometimes in an ordinary form and sometimes in a strong form. Just as you say: "So-and-so is a great eater" (*akkul*). "Akkul" is not the same as "akil" (one who eats). We all eat, and all of us are called "akil," but not all of us are called "akkul," because this form is an intensive form of the action.

If Allah is the One who manages and sustains the affairs of all the worlds of the universe, would He be "qa'im" (standing) or "qayyum" (the One who constantly sustains)? He must be "Qayyum." And "Qayyum" also means: standing by His own essence. What is the form of this standing? It is an eternal, perfect standing.

So the word "Qayyum" is an intensive form of standing over a matter. He stands by Himself, stands by His own essence, and sustains others. And the others are many and repeated. When these others are many and repeated, they need a strong attribute in their Creator, so the Creator is "Qayyum."

His saying the Truth: ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ is the support of the believer in every movement of his life. On the authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu al-Mundhir, do you know which verse of the Book of Allah is the greatest with you?" I said: "Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting." Then he struck me on the chest and said: "May knowledge be pleasant for you, O Abu al-Mundhir."

And tell us, by Allah: when there is a child and a father, does the child carry any worry about any matter of life? No, because the father takes responsibility for it. The common proverb says: "He who has a father does not carry a worry." So then, the one who has a Lord should be ashamed (to worry), because He, glorified is He, says: "I am Living, and I am Self-Subsisting," and "Qayyum" means: standing over your affairs.

He, glorified is He, affirms this self-subsistence in Surah al-Baqarah. He said in the Verse of the Throne: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾ (2:255). It is as if He is saying to us: "Sleep, you, because I do not sleep. Otherwise, if you slept and abandoned the guarding of the movement of your life, who would guard it for you?" He, glorified is He, graciously bestows upon us His self-subsistence, so ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾. And since He is "the Living" and "the Self-Subsisting," it is a logical matter that He stands over the affairs of all creation, and He has set for all creation what their lives are sustained by: material provision and the maintenance of material, and values and the maintenance of values.

And since He is the Qayyum, standing over the affair and in charge of the affairs of creation, He must deliver to them what their material requires and what sustains it, and what their values require and what sustains them. As for the requirements of matter, He says about them:

﴿And He placed firmly set mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured therein its sustenance in four days, equal for those who ask﴾ [Fussilat 41:10].

He, glorified is He, reassures us about sustenance. As for the requirements of values, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it...﴾ He, glorified is He, reassures us about sustenance. As for the requirements of values, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it...﴾

He, glory be to Him, reassures us regarding sustenance. As for the requirements of values, He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾

So He, glory be to Him, has not given us only the components of material life, but has also given us the components of values, because matter without values is fierce, wild and reckless. God wants to bring matter to a level of faith. Therefore values must be sent down. Thus He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth﴾. The form "nazzala" (نَزَّلَ) indicates something that has become obligatory upon you, because descent (nuzūl) means that something comes down from above. It says to you: do not be disdainful toward the values that have come to you from above you, because they are not from an equal of yours. They are from the Creator of the universe and of mankind. What you may be disdainful toward is what comes from one who is lower than you.

But when legislation (tashrīʿ) comes to you from one who is above you, do not be disdainful toward it, because your submission to Him is not humiliation but honour. Thus He said: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾. In the context of the Qur'an, we find Him, glory be to Him, saying:

﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 193].

And again, He says in the Noble Qur'an:

﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended, and We sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 105].

But did the Qur'an descend alone? Indeed, Jibrīl (peace be upon him) used to bring down the Qur'an upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that does not mean that the Qur'an has ceased to be "descended". Jibrīl (peace be upon him) used to bring down the Qur'an upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And the True One, exalted is He, says:

﴿And with truth We have sent it down, and with truth it has descended, and We sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 105].

Thereby "anzala" (أنزل) and "nazzala" (نزل) are equal. When we come to an event, that is, an action at any time, we ask: is it bound to a time or not bound to a time? The Noble Qur'an was sent down upon the Messenger of God Muhammad (ﷺ) over twenty-three years, and the Qur'an descends according to events, so every star (najm) of the Qur'an descends according to the requirements of occurrences. But the True One, exalted is He, says:

﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

Here the Truth specifies a time. We should know that the Qur'an which descended over twenty-three years is the same one that God sent down on the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr, the night in which the Qur'an was first revealed as a whole).

Thus the Qur'an has two descents: the first is the sending down (inzāl) from "anzala".

The other is the revelation by installments (tanzīl) from "nazzala".

So the meaning of His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree﴾ is that the Qur'an descended from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ) to the nearest heaven (al-samāʾ al-dunyā) in order to begin its mission in the universe, and this is what God sent down on the Night of Decree.

The Noble Book which God sent down on the Night of Decree to the nearest heaven descends in installments according to the events that require legislation or clarification of a matter.

But the other books did not have that kind of descent and revelation. They descended once, not according to events and occasions. They came once, just as the Qur'an first descended from the Preserved Tablet to the nearest heaven.

﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾

Let us look at the Qur'anic expression when He says:

﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 3]

Here we must notice that the Truth said of the Qur'an "nazzala" and said of the Torah and the Gospel "anzala". The transitive hamza (hamzat al-taʿdiya) has come, and He, glory be to Him, combined the Torah and the Gospel in the sending down (inzāl). This clarifies for us that God sent down the Torah and the Gospel only once, whereas the Noble Qur'an God revealed by installments over twenty-three years, suited to the events that arose in the reality of the Muslims, and containing the comprehensive message from the day of creation to the day of resurrection.

God revealed the Qur'an by installments, suited to events, in order to strengthen the heart of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because he (ﷺ) was exposed to various events. Whenever an event came that required reinforcement, a star (najm) of the Qur'an would descend.

﴿Those who disbelieve say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus [it is], that We may strengthen thereby your heart; and We have spaced it out, distinctly﴾ [al-Furqān: 32].

A star of the Qur'an would descend, and the believers would memorise it and act by its guidance, and then another star would descend. God, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And they bring you no example except that We bring you the truth and better explanation﴾ [al-Furqān: 33].

It is from His mercy, glory be to Him, toward the Muslims that He opened the way for them to ask and to seek clarification of matters that were obscure to them.

The True One, glory be to Him, made for the voluntary actions of the believers during the twenty-three years an opportunity to organise their lives in the light of the Qur'anic method. The Qur'an corrected for them whatever error had occurred. This shows that the Qur'an made argument and discussion (jadal wa munāqasha) obligatory, and made the coming of a thing at the time it is sought obligatory, because when a thing is brought at the time it is sought, the soul embraces it and is content with it.

An example of this in our daily life is that one of us may have in his home a medicine box full of various kinds of remedies, but when the owner of this box gets a little headache, he looks for an aspirin tablet. He may not know where it is in the medicine box, so he sends someone to buy it, and that is easier and more reliable.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 3, verse 4

The Truth, glory be to Him, has combined for the Qur'an between "nazzala" and "anzala," and He said: ﴿Before this, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion...﴾

The decisive word on ﴿and He sent down the Criterion﴾ will come.

Here is the combination of "nazzala" and "anzala."

And when the Truth says of the Qur'an: ﴿confirming what came before it﴾, the meaning is that the Qur'an clarifies the direction. It confirms what preceded it and what came before it. It confirms the matters of creedal faith in which no religion differs from another, because if religions differ, they differ only in some rulings. There is a ruling suited to one era and another ruling not suited to that era. As for beliefs, they do not change or alter, and likewise reports and the history of the messengers; there is no change in those matters.

The meaning of "confirming" (musaddiq) is that the report corresponds to what actually happened, and this is what we call "truthfulness" (sidq). If the report does not correspond to reality, we call it "falsehood" (kadhib). So, reality is what decides. For this reason we said earlier that the truthful person is the one whose account of events does not differ, because he draws upon a reality, and whenever he narrates the incident he narrates it exactly, with its words and details. As for the liar, there is no reality he is describing, so he creates a new reality in every account. This is why people say: "If you are a liar, then have a good memory," meaning: if you are going to lie, God forbid, then remember what you said so that you do not contradict it afterwards. The truthful person is one who investigates reality, and as long as he narrates with truthfulness, he narrates a fixed matter that desires do not twist; he does not recount one thing out of one desire and another thing out of a different desire.

And since a truthful report becomes true, because truth is the fixed thing that does not change, the Almighty says here: ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book with truth, confirming what came before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel * before, as guidance for mankind﴾.

We have spoken earlier about the Torah, and we said that some scholars, when they encounter a word, try to make it Arabic, seeking for it an Arabic pattern and an Arabic derivation. Some of them said that "Tawrat" (Torah) is from "al-warā" with a sukun on the ra', and people in ancient times would kindle fire by striking one stick against another, saying: "the tinder has kindled (waraa)," meaning its fire has come out. Some scholars also said that "Injil" (Gospel) is from "al-najl," which means increase.

I say to those scholars: you have looked at these words as if they were Arabic words. But "Tawrat" is a Hebrew word, and "Injil" is a Syriac or Greek word, and those words became names for those books and entered our language. Do not think that because the Qur'an was revealed in Arabic, all its words are Arabic. No. It is true that the Qur'an is Arabic, and it is also true that it came while these words were current on the tongue of the Arabs, and when they are pronounced their meaning is understood.

An example of this is that in the modern era we have introduced the word "bank" into the language and spoken it, and it became Arabic because it circulates on the Arabic tongue. So the meaning of the Qur'an being Arabic is that when God addressed the Arabs, He addressed them with words they understood, which were current on their tongues, even if they were not originally Arabic. When the Truth spoke of the Torah and the Gospel and said that the Qur'an came confirming them, He, may His majesty be exalted, said:

﴿Before this, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4]

Who are these people of whom He said ﴿guidance for mankind﴾? Undoubtedly they are the people who were contemporaries of the call of those books. And if the Qur'an came confirming what is in the Torah and the Gospel, are these books not guidance for us too? Yes, they are guidance for us, but guidance comes through the Qur'an's confirmation of them, so that whatever is in them and attributed to them does not become a proof against us. What the Qur'an confirms is the proof against us. So ﴿guidance for mankind﴾ means: those who were contemporaries of these religions and these books, and we believe in what is in them through the Qur'an's confirmation of them.

When the Almighty, exalted is He, says "and He sent down the Criterion," this indicates that the Book, that is the Qur'an, would coincide with a difficult mission. The word "Criterion" (al-furqan) only comes where there is a battle, and we want to distinguish between two matters: guidance and misguidance, truth and falsehood, misery and happiness, uprightness and deviation. So the word "Criterion" indicates that the Qur'an came to undertake a difficult mission, namely that it distinguishes between good and evil. And since it distinguishes between good and evil, there is good and it has a camp, and there is evil and it has a camp, so there are two groups. It comes to the group that defends the truth with struggle and jihad, by which it distinguishes and separates truth from falsehood. The Truth concludes this verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution.﴾

Why did this closing come in this form in this verse? That is, since the Qur'an is a Criterion, it must distinguish between truth and falsehood. The truth has its soldiers, who are the believers, and falsehood has its soldiers, who are the disbelievers, and evil has come from the disbelievers, so it must speak of those who disbelieved: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment﴾. Punishment is pain, and it differs in strength and weakness according to the direct inflicter of the punishment. The slap of a child is not the slap of a young man, and not the slap of a strong man; each one delivers the slap according to his strength. So if the punishment issues from the strength of the Strong, who is God, then it must be a punishment that cannot be endured. ﴿They will have a severe punishment, and God is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾, meaning He cannot be overcome in His affair, there is no other power against Him, and no one can repel His retribution.

As for the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him, that He is "Qayyum," meaning He takes care of the affairs of His creation, bringing them into existence and sustaining them, creating matter and establishing its values, it must follow from this that He knows all creation and knows the hidden things, and therefore He sets the appropriate legislation for everything that happens to them. The legislations that come from humans differ from the legislations that come from God. Why?

Because when God legislates through a Book that He sends down to His messenger to convey God's ruling in it, He, glory be to Him, legislates for what He knows, and what He knows He may make known to His creation or they may not know it, and events may come about that were not in the mind of the human legislator when he legislated, so they are usually compelled to change the law, because events have occurred that the human legislator did not take into account.

Why did the human legislator not take them into account? Because his knowledge is confined to the visible things existing in his era, and he is not contemporary with the things that happen after his era, and also he legislates for faculties hidden from him.

Since the Almighty, glory be to Him, is Qayyum, and He sends down what distinguishes truth from falsehood, He, glory be to Him, knows with a vast knowledge, such that no correction can be made upon Him. Therefore, those who try to say that this ruling is not suitable for the age, we say to them: do you correct God? As if you are saying that God has missed such an account and you want to correct it for Him!

No, do not correct God; take God's ruling as it is, because this is the ruling that falsehood does not reach from before it or behind it, since it is the ruling of a Knower whose knowledge does not renew and nothing arises in His knowledge. Above all that, He, glory be to Him, does not benefit from what He legislates, and He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from God﴾.

Look at how this verse serves all the preceding themes: since He is al-Qayyum (the Self-Subsisting, who sustains and manages all creation), He must know everything about His creation, so nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him. And since He will distinguish between truth and falsehood and inflict a severe punishment upon the disbelievers, nothing is hidden from Him. The verse serves every purpose, and He, glorified is He, knows every purpose. When He legislates by His self-subsistence, He legislates without anyone being able to overrule Him, and when anyone departs from His method, it is not hidden from Him. Thus the verse is a harvest of both legislation and recompense: ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 6:

Then, after that, the Truth speaks of the first manifestation of His self-subsistence (al-qayyumiyyah) in relation to man, saying: ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills...﴾ ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

The forming (taswir) in the womb is the bringing into existence of the matter from which the human being will come into being in a particular form. This form differs in its kind: maleness and femaleness. And maleness and femaleness differ in their shapes: white, dark, wheat-coloured, reddish, short, and tall. These are the forms in which creation exists, and among them is:

﴿And the difference of your tongues and your colours﴾ [al-Rum: 22].

This difference in colours, tongues and the many other things indicates that they are not the product of a factory that makes a mould and then shapes things upon it. No! Every human being is born, shaped by a capable hand, by an inherent power.

Now, if a craftsman wants to make you a cup, he makes a mould and repeats it. But in human creation, each one has his own mould, each one has his particular form, each one has his particular voice, which has been proven to have a fingerprint like the fingerprint of the hand, and each one has a colour. So these are among the signs, and this is evidence of the absolute power of God. And above all this, it is a creation that does not need a process of treatment. The meaning of a process of treatment is that one makes a single mould into which one pours its matter. No, He, majestic is His glory, says:

﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117].

The father and mother may share the same colour, yet the son may grow up with a different colour. God creates most people in sound form, and He creates a few people in unsound form; a child may be born blind, or afflicted with some defect, or with an extra finger or two fingers... And this anomaly, God willed it in creation so that the Truth might draw our attention to the goodness and beauty of His creation. For the one who is sound sees another person hindered from movement, and so he praises God for his complete creation.

When a person who has five fingers on each hand sees another person with an extra finger that hinders the movement of his hand, he knows the wisdom in the existence of the five fingers. Beauty is established only through the existence of ugliness, and things are distinguished by their opposites. A person who has seven fingers on one hand places medicine before a task to which it devotes itself, so that the doctor can remove what is in excess of the needs of the normal human being. And had God created the human being with three fingers, that person would not have been able to control himself when using fine objects.

The ordinary person in his daily movement does not perceive the beauty of the soundness of his creation unless he sees an individual from among the examples of anomaly. The Truth draws the attention of people who are heedless of God's blessings upon them, because of their routine, by their loss in others. So when a seeing person sees a blind man walking with a cane, he becomes aware of the blessing of sight that God has granted him, and so he feels God's blessing upon him. Anomaly in creation is an illustrative pattern that draws people's attention to the blessings with which God has favoured them.

These examples in the universe draw people's attention to God's blessings in them, and that is why you find them before you. Also, so that you do not object to your Creator and do not say: "What is the fault of this person that he should be created like this?" He, glory be to Him, will compensate him in another respect; He may give him a genius that surpasses the capacities of the one who sees.

We strike this example, and to God belongs the highest example, of the one who wandered the world, "Timur Lenk the Lame," the commander who astonished the world with his courage. God gave him the gift of planning and fighting as compensation for his lameness. And we find that geniuses burst forth most often among the anomalous. Why? Because God gives the one who is incapacitated in a certain way an aspiration that tries to compensate for what he has lost in something else, and so brilliance comes. Therefore, ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾, and every formation has a wisdom. And since every formation has a wisdom, all of God's creation is beautiful.

You must not take creation separated from the wisdom of its Creator; rather, take every creation together with its wisdom. What makes you say, "This is ugly," is that you separate the created thing from its wisdom. An example of this: a pupil who fails may grieve his father, but why do you take the failure away from its wisdom? He failed so that he might learn the meaning of seriousness in study. If he had passed while playing, what would happen? All his peers who learned that he played and passed would play and say: "This one played and passed..." Therefore, you must take every deed together with the wisdom of its existence.

Likewise, do not take the punishment separated from the crime. Every punishment, we must take it joined to its crime. When you see someone, for example, whom they are going to sentence to execution, mercy for him takes hold of you and you grieve. Here we say to you: you have separated his execution from the murder he committed earlier. Rather, if you recalled his crime, you would find that he is being killed in justice and retribution, for he killed another unjustly. So do not separate this from that.

﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but He﴾. The meaning of ﴿There is no god but He﴾ is: He forms, and He knows that what He forms will be in this form; for there is no other god who says to Him, "This does not please me, and I will form another form." No; because the One who does this is Mighty, meaning He is not overcome in a matter, and everything He wills happens, and every command of His is for a wisdom. Because when He says ﴿He forms you in the wombs﴾, someone among people may say: there are abnormal forms and unnatural forms. And He, glory be to Him, says to you: I am the Wise, and I do things for a wisdom, so do not separate the event from its wisdom. Take the event with its wisdom, and if you take the event with its wisdom, you will find it to be beauty itself. And He, glory be to Him, is the One who forms in the womb however He wills; this is with regard to its matter.

Al-Sha'rawi, the commentary continues:

He, glory be to Him, makes clear: He will not leave matter as it is, but will set for this matter values (qiyam) so that the movement of existence harmonizes with itself. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat)—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

So, after He has shaped us in the wombs as He wills, according to the requirement of His wisdom, He will not leave forms without a method of values. Rather, He made the method of values by sending down the Qur'an, in which is the method of values. We must take a thing together with its wisdom, and when we take a thing together with its wisdom, every matter stands upright, all of it beautiful and all of it good. He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive.﴾

What does the Truth mean by His words ﴿verses that are decisive (muhkamat)﴾? The decisive thing is that into which no defect or corruption in understanding can seep, because it is decisive. These decisive verses are the texts about which people do not differ. When He says:

﴿As for the thief, male or female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38].

This is a verse containing a clear ruling. And He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿The adulteress and the adulterer—flog each one of them﴾ [al-Nur: 2].

These too are clear matters. This is what is decisive among the verses. The decisive is that about which understandings do not differ, because its text is clear and explicit and admits of no other meaning. And "the allegorical" (mutashabih) is that whose intended meaning we toil to understand. Since we will toil to understand its intended meaning, why did He send it down?

As I told you, He makes clear—take a thing together with its wisdom so that you know why it was revealed. The decisive verses came for the rulings required of creation, namely: do this, and do not do that. Since these are actions required of creation, the one who performs them is rewarded, and the one who does not perform them is punished. Thus reward and punishment follow from them, and they come in a clear form; otherwise someone would say, "I did not understand." The rulings say to you: "Do this and do not do that." When they say "Do," you are capable of not doing; for had you been created only to do, He would not say to you "Do." But because you are capable of doing and of not doing, He says to you "Do."

And when He says to you "Do not do," you are capable of doing; so it is not said "Do and do not do" except because He created in you the capacity to do or not to do. We note that when He says to me "Do this and do not do that," He wants me to stand before the desire of my soul in doing and in refraining. For this reason the Truth says concerning prayer:

﴿And indeed it is burdensome except for the humble (khashi'in)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 45].

So when He says to me "Do and do not do," the meaning is that there are things that are heavy for me to do, and that something heavy for me to refrain from. For example, the eye was created by God capable of seeing everything within its range, according to the law of light, and the Truth says to it:

﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 101].

But regarding a woman whom it is not lawful for you to look at, the Truth says: lower (your gaze).

﴿Say to the believing men that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts; that is purer for them. Indeed Allah is Acquainted with what they do. And say to the believing women that they lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ [al-Nur: 30–31].

The meaning of ﴿yaghuddu﴾ and ﴿yaghdudna﴾ is that He, glory be to Him, has specified the movement of the eye. Another example: the hand moves, and He commands you not to move it except in what is commanded, so you do not strike anyone with it, nor kindle with it a fire that burns and corrupts, but kindle with it a fire to cook, for instance.

So He, glory be to Him, comes with "do and do not do" and specifies the desires of the soul in doing or refraining. If the desire of the soul is to sleep, the worshipful command says: Arise and pray. If the desire of the soul is to become angry, the faith-based command says: Do not be angry.

Thus the ruling came with "do and do not do" to regulate the movement of the human being, for he may want to do a harmful act, so He says to him: Do not do it; and he may want not to do a good act, so He says to him: Do it. Thus all human movements are governed by "do and do not do." Your intellect is one of the means of perception, like the eye, the ear, and the tongue. The task of the intellect is to perceive; its duty calls it to understand one matter and not to understand another. And God made the decisive verses to relieve the intellect of the task of searching for the wisdom of every decisive command, since it may rise above human perception. The Truth wants to bind the servant to the manners of obedience even in matters whose legislative wisdom is not perceived, and also to set your intellect in motion to refer every allegorical verse back to the decisive verses.

When we read the Truth's words:

﴿No vision can grasp Him, but He grasps all vision, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-An'am: 103].

we see that this is a general statement. And in another verse He says:

﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23].

And speaking of the disbelievers He says:

﴿No indeed! Surely they, that day, will be veiled from their Lord﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15].

Thus the intellect is occupied with His words ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾, and this applies in this world. As for the Hereafter, the human being will have been prepared with a different preparation so as to see God. We are now in this world in the manner in which God has prepared us to live in this world, and we cannot see God. The matter of preparing something to perform a function for which it is not now qualified or equipped exists in our world. We know that a blind person undergoes surgery or is fitted with corrective glasses and then sees. And for one who does not hear or is hard of hearing, we make a hearing aid for him and he hears with it.

So if humans have been able, by their own capacities in the material universe, to prepare things that qualify them to regain some sense, how much more so the Most Generous Creator, the Lord who nurtures: is He not able to re-create us in the Hereafter in a manner that enables us to see His Essence and His Face?! He is capable of all things.

So the matter here is allegorical: whether God is "yudraku" (perceived, with a dammah on the yā' and a fatḥah on the rā') or "lā yudraku" (not perceived), what has changed in the rulings for you? Nothing. So these allegorical verses did not come for the sake of rulings; they came for the sake of faith alone. For this reason the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, ends every scholarly dispute over this matter by saying, he being the Seal of the Prophets:

"The Qur'an was not sent down so that some of it would contradict other parts. So what you know of it, act upon; and what is allegorical in it, believe in it."

The allegorical verses came to be believed in, and the decisive verses came to be acted upon, and the believer must always refer the allegorical to the decisive. An example of this: when we hear the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is above their hands. So whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah—He will give him a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 10].

A person may ask: "Does God have a hand?" The human being must refer this to the sphere of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. When the believer hears the Truth's words:

﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5].

Does God have a body by which He settles on a throne? Here we say: this is the allegorical matter which the believer must believe in, for your existence, O human, is not like the existence of God, your hand is not like the hand of God, and your being established is likewise not like God's being established. Since His existence is not like your existence and His life is not like your life, why would you want His hand to be like your hand?

He is as He described Himself: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. And why did God introduce us into those domains? Because God wants to draw His creatures' attention to matters that may not sit well with the intellects; so whoever's understanding is broad enough to interpret and refer them to the decisive, by holding that nothing is like unto Him, that is his right. And whoever's understanding is broad and says: "I believe that God has a hand, but within the framework of ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾," that too is his right, and this is safer.

And the Truth says: ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are decisive verses, they are the foundation of the Book.﴾ The meaning of ﴿umm﴾ is the origin to which the interpretation of the allegorical must ultimately return, if you interpret it, or you refer it back to the decisive, saying: God has a hand, but not like the hands of human beings. You enter thereby within the scope of:

﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11].

And why did the Truth say ﴿they are the foundation (umm) of the Book﴾ and not "they are the mothers (ummahat) of the Book"? You should know, O believer, that not each one of them is a mother, but their totality is the mother. To clarify this, let us hear the Truth's words:

﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign, and We sheltered them on a height, a place of rest and springs﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50].

The Truth did not say "they are two signs," because Jesus, peace be upon him, did not come into being as a sign except by his birth from his mother without a father, that is, together with his mother; and his mother was not a sign except by the birth of Jesus, that is, together with Jesus. So the two together constitute the sign. Likewise, ﴿they are the foundation of the Book, and others are allegorical﴾: what is meant is not that each decisive verse is a mother of the Book; rather, the decisive verses in their entirety are the foundation, and the origin to which the believer refers any allegorical matter. The task of the decisive is that we act upon it, and the task of the allegorical is that we believe in it; the proof is that however you conceive it, it does not affect your action.

So the Truth's words ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ entail no ruling; here faith alone suffices.

But what of those of whom Allah said: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is allegorical in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾? We should know that "zaygh" is inclination; "zaagha" means he inclined, and it is derived from the "tazayyugh" of the teeth, that is, the difference in their growth: one tooth appears inward, another outward. When teeth do not grow straight, people now perform cosmetic and orthodontic procedures to make them one straight row.

Those whose hearts have deviation, that is inclination, follow what is allegorical among the verses, seeking discord. It is as if deviation is something that befalls hearts, and it is not the origin that hearts have deviation; for the sound nature has no deviation in it, but desires are what make hearts incline, and a person may know God's correct ruling on a matter, yet his desire overcomes him and he inclines away from God's ruling. Inclination is a product of the heart; a person may subject his logic and thought to serve the inclination of his heart. For this reason the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, says: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought."

Why? Because the bane of opinion is desire. Even deviants know the sound intention, but one of them deviates because of what he desires; and the evidence that a deviant knows the sound intention is that after he has taken his fill of deviation, he repents and announces his repentance, and this is well known in many cases; for inclination is a forced, rationalizing effort, whereas the sound intention is a natural matter that does not exhaust. An example: when a person looks at what is lawful for him, he finds no emotion of one faculty contradicting the emotion of another; but when he looks at a woman who is not his wife, his faculties fight, and he asks himself:

And as for "those firmly grounded in knowledge" (al-Rasikhun fi al-'Ilm), when they distinguished the matter of the ambiguous (al-mutashabih), they called upon God with the words He revealed: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾

So the saying of those firmly grounded in knowledge amounts to this: every clear (muhkam) verse and every ambiguous (mutashabih) verse is from God; we act upon the clear, and we believe in the ambiguous. This is guidance. Then comes the supplication for steadfastness upon this guidance. The meaning is: O Lord, keep us steadfast in Your worship, and do not let our hearts incline or swerve.

This shows us that hearts turn and change. Therefore the decisive word comes in the form of supplication for steadfastness in faith:

﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8].

They ask for mercy as a gift (hibah), not mercy as a right (haqq). No created being has any right over God except what God has bestowed upon him. Those firmly grounded in knowledge ask God for mercy that protects them from falling into desire (hawa) after God has guided them to this sound judgment, that the ambiguous and the clear are all from God. And they teach us how the path to guidance is, and how to seek the mercy of gift.

The learned ones who are firmly rooted in knowledge, since they have understood something, want to spread it among people. Therefore they say to us:

Beware lest you think the matter is only a matter of understanding a text, and it ends there. Rather, the matter has another consequence that follows from it, and this other consequence does not exist only in this world, for there is the Hereafter. The world is within one's capacity because it is limited in duration and finite, but there is the Hereafter, which comes after the world, where there is eternity. So the Truth (al-Haqq) says, on the tongue of those firmly rooted in knowledge: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of the people for a Day about which there is no doubt...﴾

Their saying ﴿Our Lord﴾ (Rabbana) tells us that He is the Truth who undertakes nurture (tarbiyah), and the meaning of nurture is bringing the one being nurtured to the perfection required for him. So there is a Lord who nurtures, and there is a servant who is being nurtured, and the Lord gives a person what qualifies him for the perfection required for him.

The believers call upon God, saying: O Lord, among the completeness of Your nurturing of us is that You protect us from the punishment of the Hereafter. So when we have lived this world and it has ended, we know that You are the gatherer of the people for a Day about which there is no doubt, and since You are Lord, and since You are God, You do not break the promise. For the one who breaks a promise cannot be a god, because a god, at the time of promising, knows with the completeness of His power and the perfection of His knowledge that He is able to fulfil it. As for one who does not have the power to fulfil, he cannot make a promise except qualified by something he relies upon, like our saying, we servants: "God willing" (in sha' Allah). Why? Because one of us cannot guarantee to fulfil what he has promised.

When we were confronted with the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted be He:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," * Except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right conduct."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24]

We said: beware lest you say, "I will do such-and-such," unless you attach it to and link it with the will of God, for if you promise, you do not guarantee your life or the fulfilment of your promise. You will not do anything except by the will of God. Therefore do not promise except with the will (of God), because you promise what you do not guarantee. In reality, you own nothing. If you wish to do any action or go to any place, the act requires an agent, an object, a time, a place, and a cause, and then it requires power to carry out the act. A human being possesses none of these things except what God wills him to possess. A human being cannot continue to be the agent. A human being cannot, when the agent exists, bring about the object. A human being does not possess time, and does not possess place; indeed, a human being cannot keep the cause in existence so as to do what he wanted to do. All these elements, the agent, the object, the time, the place, and the cause, belong to God alone. Therefore let a person protect himself from being a liar and a presumptuous gambler, and let him be under the shade of His saying, exalted be He:

﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," * Except [when adding], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right conduct."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23-24]

The phrase ﴿except that Allah wills﴾ (illa an yasha'a Allah) protects a person from being a liar. When what a person promised does not happen, that means God did not will it, because a person does not possess a single element of this act. When the Truth says: ﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not break the promise﴾, this is because one who breaks a promise is only prevented by some overpowering force that comes upon him, even if it is a change in his own self that prevents him from acting. As for God, no overpowering force comes to change what He wills to do, and it is impossible for Him to change, because change is not an attribute of the eternal, the Everlasting.

And when the Truth affirms that we will be gathered by His will on a Day about which there is no doubt, and that God does not break the promise, it is certain that we will meet. And why will we meet? The learned ones firmly rooted in knowledge said: we act upon the clear (muhkam) and believe in the ambiguous (mutashabih), and they called upon God to make their hearts steadfast upon guidance, as a mercy from Him, and to keep their hearts far from deviation, because they fear the Day on which God will gather the people. Indeed, we will meet for reckoning concerning our deeds and our faith.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 10:

After that, the Truth, may His majesty be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will never avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all...﴾

At the moment you hear it, you who are a believer, the disbeliever hears it with you, and the hypocrite hears it with you: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You are the Gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾ Perhaps the disbeliever or the hypocrite thinks that there is something that may rescue him from what will happen on that day, such as the support of children, or abundant wealth with which he might ransom himself, or friendship, or intercession. Here the Truth says to them: No, your children and your wealth will not avail you anything.

In the language, it is said: "This thing does not avail so-and-so," meaning that he remains in need of others, because ghina' (sufficiency, wealth) is not needing others. Wealth and children do not make anyone sufficient on the Day of Resurrection. In that matter there is no support, and there are no kinship ties among them on that day. Paradise is not for sale, so no one can buy a place in Paradise with wealth he owns.

The disbelievers in the days of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say that unusual statement: "Since Allah has given us wealth and children in this world, He must give us in the Hereafter something better than that." Therefore Allah says to them: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth will never avail them, nor their children, against Allah at all.﴾ So the whole matter is referred back to Allah. It is true that in this world Allah may create the causes, and the disbeliever is governed by causes, and so is the believer; if the disbeliever takes the causes, he obtains the result. But in the Hereafter the matter is different; no one will possess causes. Therefore the Truth says about the Last Day:

﴿The Day they will come forth, nothing of them will be hidden from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion this Day?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer."﴾ [Ghafir: 16].

In this world, people possess causes and live differing in bliss according to their different causes, and according to the differing of their striving in life, and the differing availability of what gives a person pleasures. But the matter in the Hereafter has no striving and no causes, because the believing person in the Hereafter lives by the Causer, who is Allah, glorified is His power; so the moment a thing occurs to the believer's mind in Paradise, the thing comes to him. As for the disbelievers, their wealth and their children do not avail them, because they were occupied in this world with wealth and children and disbelieved in Allah.

﴿The ones left behind among the Bedouins will say to you, "Our wealth and our families occupied us, so ask forgiveness for us." They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts.﴾ [al-Fath: 11].

So what the disbelievers were occupied with in this world will not benefit them. And the Truth adds, concerning the disbelievers, in the appendix to the verse we are dealing with: ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire.﴾ They are the ones who will be punished, and they will be tormented in the Fire. Let us observe the severe retribution upon them: those who are punished are themselves the ones who punish, because they themselves will be the fuel of the Fire. The mu'adhdhab (the one punished), with a fatha on the ʿayn and a fatha on the dhāl with shaddah, is the mu'adhdhib (the one punishing), with a fatha on the ʿayn and a kasra on the dhāl with shaddah.

This is the revolt of the parts. The atoms of the disbeliever are believing, the atoms of the sinner are obedient, and what made these atoms turn toward doing what angers Allah is the will of their owner over them.

In ancient times we coined an example, and to Allah belongs the highest example, and we said: Suppose a battalion has a commander. It is required of the battalion that it hear the commander's order and carry out what it was commanded. If they come, when the supreme commander is over them, they raise their matter to him and say: "By the order we carried out the work that was issued to us by our immediate commander, and we were not in agreement with his opinion." And in the life of faith we find the wise saying of the Creator:

﴿On the Day their tongues, their hands, and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do.﴾ [al-Nur: 24].

So the tongue speaks the word of disbelief while it curses its owner, and the hand advances toward disobedience while it is averse to its owner and cursing him. The supreme will of Allah is what gave the disbeliever a will over his hand and tongue in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection Allah will strip the disbeliever's will from his limbs, so they will testify against him that he compelled them to commit sins, and the parts will punish one another. When the Truth says: ﴿And those are the fuel of the Fire,﴾ there is a matter we must heed and take from the reality of history. This matter is that those who disbelieved in the messages of Allah on earth received some of the punishment in this world, because Allah does not store up all the punishment for the Hereafter; otherwise people would be wretched because of the disbelievers and the sinners. Therefore Allah hastens some of the punishment for the disbelievers and sinners in this world.

The Truth gives an example of this: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 11:

﴿As the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins, and Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

When you hear "kadab kadha" (as the case of such-and-such), then "da'b" (habit, constant pattern) is the act pursued with effort and without interruption. We say: "So-and-so's da'b is to do such-and-such," meaning he is constantly accustomed to doing such-and-such. Or we say: "So-and-so has no da'b except backbiting people."

Does this mean that all his actions are confined to backbiting people, or that he performs other actions? He performs other actions, but backbiting predominates over him, and this is his da'b. So da'b is striving with effort and continuity until the act, through repetition, becomes a habit. Thus His saying, the Truth: ﴿as the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾ means as the habit of the people of Pharaoh. The people of Pharaoh were a people who came before the Islamic message, and before them were the people of Thamud, 'Ad and others.

The Truth, glory be to Him, draws our attention to look at these people and see what happened to them. He, glory be to Him, did not postpone their punishment to the Hereafter, because people might think that Allah has stored up the punishment of the disbelievers for the Hereafter, since He said:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them at all against Allah; and they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 10].

No, rather the punishment is also in this world, in confirmation of His saying, the Truth:

﴿For them is a punishment in the worldly life, and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe, and they will have from Allah no protector﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 34].

If the punishment were postponed to the Hereafter, people would be made wretched along with the wretched. Therefore Allah brings examples from life and says: ﴿as the case of the people of Pharaoh﴾, that is, as the habit of the people of Pharaoh. A matter does not become a habit except through striving in work, and the da'b of the people of Pharaoh was denial, tyranny, and Pharaoh's claim to divinity.

He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And those before them denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins, and Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ So the da'b became theirs, and what befell them. If they had become accustomed to disbelief and denial, then Allah inflicted punishment upon them. The da'b of the people of Pharaoh was denial, and the Creator, glory be to Him, requites them for that by punishing them. And read, if you wish, the saying of the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted:

﴿By the dawn, and by ten nights, and by the even and the odd, and by the night when it passes. Is there in that an oath for one of understanding? Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, Iram of the pillars, the like of which was not created in the lands, and Thamud who hewed out the rocks in the valley, and Pharaoh of the stakes? Those who transgressed in the lands and increased therein corruption. So your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment. Indeed, your Lord is ever in observation.﴾ [al-Fajr: 1-14].

So their da'b was denial, and Allah's requital for it was punishment and retribution. Thus His saying, the Truth: ﴿So Allah seized them for their sins, and Allah is severe in punishment﴾ means He inflicted punishment upon them in this world, and the end was what it was for the people of Pharaoh, Thamud, and those before them from the disbelieving people.

When you hear the saying of Allah: ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment﴾, the mind turns to there being a sin that deserves punishment. All matters of the abstract are always drawn from the sensible, because the origin of forming any abstract knowledge is sensory observation, and sensible things are then transferred to the abstract afterward.

Why? Because a sensible thing is witnessed by all, whereas an abstract thing is understood only by those who reason, and a human being has many stages. In the stage of childhood, a person understands and comprehends only what is physically before him.

I said long ago regarding the meaning of the word "ghasb" (usurpation): it is taking and stripping something from a person who has a right, by force. This is an abstract matter that has a visual image, because the one who strips the skin from a sheep we call a usurper (ghasib). Let us see how taking a right from its owner occurs: it is exactly like flaying, and the word comes for clarification.

The word "dhamb" (sin) and the word "'uqubah" (punishment) are interlinked: the word "dhamb" is derived from the root dh-n-b, because the whole root indicates "that which follows," and the dhanab (tail) follows the front part in an animal. And 'iqab is what comes after a thing.

So there is a sin, and there is a punishment. But what comes before the sin, and what follows the punishment? There is no sin except when a text exists that criminalizes it; so there is no sin except by a text. Not every act is a sin; there must be a text before the sin occurs that criminalizes its act. Therefore positive law has adopted this matter, and says: a person cannot be punished except by criminalization, and there is no criminalization except by a text. It is not possible for someone to come suddenly and say: this act is a crime for which one is punished. Rather, there must be warning and a text beforehand criminalizing this act.

There is no punishment except by criminalization, and no criminalization except by a text. The text clarifies the criminalization of a type of act, and if a person commits this act, he is criminalized, and that is the sin; so the sin is as though it came following the text of criminalization. Punishment comes after the crime, and thus we find that both sin and crime take on the actual wording, its signification, and its meaning: the dhanab is that which follows a thing. For this reason they call the bucket with which they draw water "dhanub," because it follows the rope. Also the recompense in the Hereafter:

﴿For those who did wrong there is a portion like the portion of their companions, so let them not seek to hasten Me﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 59].

That is, dhunub (portions) that follow and succeed their crime. Thus the Qur'anic text regarding any sin and any punishment confirms for us the technical legal principle found throughout the world: there is no punishment without criminalization. So punishment comes after the crime, that is, after the sin, and the sin is part of the text; so we do not come to anyone without a prior text and say to him: you have committed a sin. This resolves many difficulties, for example:

﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills. And whoever associates partners with Allah has invented a tremendous sin﴾ [an-Nisa': 48].

Allah forgives what is below associating partners with Him; associating partners with Allah is the supreme treason, and there is no forgiveness for it; and beyond that He forgives whom He wills. The Truth says in another verse:

﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ [az-Zumar: 53].

Some people say: Allah said that He does not forgive that He be associated with, and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills, to the point that they say: when this verse came in which the Truth said ﴿Indeed, Allah forgives all sins﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: "except shirk," so that this verse would not clash with the other verse.

In reality, when people of understanding examine it carefully, they will find no clash, because those who transgressed against themselves are among the servants of Allah who believed and did not associate anyone with their Lord, but they slipped, went astray, and fell into sins. These are said to be sinners, because they are believers in Allah and acknowledge what He sent down; but the polytheist has not acknowledged Allah nor what He legislated and ordained of rulings, so what he is upon is not called a sin but disbelief and shirk. There is no contradiction or clash in the verses of the Most Merciful.

And when the Truth says: ﴿As the case of the people of Pharaoh and those before them: they denied Our signs, so Allah seized them for their sins, and Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 11].

This wise statement is balanced and consistent: the sin comes after a text, and the punishment after that.

Almighty God commands His Messenger to convey to the disbelievers: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place."﴾

This is a command from God to His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and he is the one who conveys from God. He is to bring to the disbelievers a message containing a warning. Who are these disbelievers? Are they the disbelievers of Quraysh? That is permissible. Are they the Jews? That is permissible too. The conveyance (al-balagh) therefore encompasses every disbeliever.

The Qur'anic text, when it comes, comes in a manner different from people's usual mode of address. To give an example, and to God belongs the highest likeness, and He is exalted above comparison or similitude: you say to your son, "Go to your uncle and say to him: My father will visit you tomorrow." What then will the son's speech to the uncle be? The son goes to the uncle and says, "My father will visit you tomorrow." But the one giving the order, who is the father, says, "Tell your uncle that my father will visit you tomorrow." If the son is scrupulously faithful, he says:

"My father said: Tell your uncle that my father will visit you tomorrow."

And when God, glorified is He, says ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾,

this means the utmost fidelity on the part of the Messenger who conveys from God: he transmitted to the disbelievers the text which God had commanded him to convey to them. Otherwise, it would have been sufficient for the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to go to the disbelievers and say to them: "You will be overcome and gathered." But who could know that this speech was not from Muhammad, who is a human being? Therefore the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, conveys to them that God has informed him to convey to them with His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾.

The Messenger did not convey it in his own words; no. Rather, he conveyed to them the exact text of the message with which God sent him. When God, in His Qur'an, commands His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, to convey a command to the disbelievers, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is addressed, and the disbelievers are addressed; so when he confronts them, he says to them: "You will be overcome..." And in another verse God says:

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: If they desist, what has passed will be forgiven them; but if they return, then the precedent of the former peoples has already gone before them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38].

The analogy would be for him to say: "If you desist, what has passed will be forgiven you." But God said: ﴿If they desist﴾, so it is as if, when God spoke, the disbelievers were not present for the address, and the Messenger of God was the one present for the address, while God was speaking about absent persons.

But God, in this verse which we are discussing, charges the Messenger with complete conveyance: sometimes the transmission is from the First Commander exactly as it was issued from Him, such as His saying ﴿If they desist﴾; and sometimes the First Commander orders him to convey the word by which he is the one addressing them, meaning: do not say "they will be overcome," but say ﴿You will be overcome﴾, because you are the one who will address them. This precision in delivery can only come from the All-Powerful, the All-Wise.

It is a conveyance to the disbelievers of Quraysh or to the disbelievers in general. The overcoming will be in this world, and the gathering will be in the Hereafter.

If the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was transmitting the Qur'anic text ﴿You will be overcome﴾, when did the Messenger say it? He said it while the Muslims were few and unable to protect themselves, and could do nothing.

Every believer lives under the protection of another, or emigrates to a distant place. Could such a message come except from one who possesses all means?

The Messenger said it as one conveying from God, while the Muslims were in an evident state of weakness; and since he said it, it is a proof against them, because the one who conveyed it, namely God, is able to do it. ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome﴾ — the punishment is not only in this world, but in the Hereafter too: ﴿and you will be gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting place﴾. This matter is good tidings to the Messenger of God and his companions, and a warning to the disbelievers in him, and it was fulfilled at the Battle of Badr. When the verse of God was revealed:

﴿The multitude will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45],

our master 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked: "What multitude is this?" He knew that the Muslims were weak and could not do that, and that the causes of the Muslims' victory did not exist; but the Messenger of God did not address the believers through causes, but through the Lord of causes. So when he challenged and warned them, although he and his companions were weak before them, reality came to confirm the truth of God's word: ﴿You will be overcome﴾, and the Muslims' victory indeed occurred, and they overcame the disbelievers.

Should not the truthfulness of the Messenger's conveyance in what happens in this world be taken as proof of its truthfulness regarding what happens in the Hereafter? The fulfillment of ﴿You will be overcome﴾ confirms ﴿and you will be gathered into Hell﴾. In this verse there are two things: first, a conveyance about the defeat of the disbelievers in this world, which is a matter that all people witness; and the second matter is in the Hereafter, which some people may deny. If God has informed His Messenger, "O Muhammad, you will overcome the disbelievers," while you do not possess the means of overcoming them, and then the course of events comes and confirms that the disbelievers were defeated, then since the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was truthful in conveying the first, and did not possess the means, it must be that he is truthful in conveying the second, which is the gathering into the fire of Hell.

Some exegetes have said that this statement was addressed to the Jews, because when the Muslims were victorious at Badr, the Jews were shaken with a severe shaking, for they were not confident that Islam and the Muslims would win at Badr. When Islam triumphed at Badr, some Jews said: "Muhammad is the Prophet whom God promised us, and it is better for us to believe in him." But a group of them said: "Wait for another battle." That is, do not take it from the first battle; wait. Then the Battle of Uhud came, and the war was back and forth.

And we may say: what prevents the verse from being addressed to the Jews, the polytheists, and those who disbelieve in general? The wording is general. It is also reported that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, gathered the Jews in the market of Banu Qaynuqa' and said to them: "O assembly of Jews, beware of what befell Quraysh, and submit before there befalls you what befell them. You know that I am a sent Prophet." What did they say to him? They said: "Do not let it deceive you that you met a people who are inexperienced (aghmar), that is, people of the common folk who have not tried affairs and have no knowledge of war, so you seized an opportunity against them. If you fight us, you will know that we are the [real] people." Then God revealed His words: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome..﴾ to the end of the verse.

Al-mihad is what is commonly prepared for a child so that he may sleep on it in a settled manner, that is, it has a resting place. The phrase ﴿and wretched is the resting place﴾ indicates that they have no capacity to change what they are in, just as a child has no ability to resist whoever places him to sleep in any place.

Then the Truth (Allah) says after that: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met: one host fighting in the way of Allah, and another, disbelieving...﴾

When the Truth says: ﴿There has already been a sign for you﴾, who is addressed by this verse? Undoubtedly, the one addressed by this verse is everyone whose life came after this event, whether believer or disbeliever. For the believer, it is confirmed that Allah's victory comes even without (apparent) causes, and for the disbeliever, the verse comes as a lesson that Allah forsakes him even with (all) the causes. Allah made that encounter a sign. The sign (āyah) is the wondrous thing, meaning that its occurrence and its results do not come in accordance with human premises.

Yes, this is a general address to everyone who belongs to either of the two fighting groups, whether the group of faith or the group of disbelief. For the group of faith, so that it understands that material causes are not everything in the battle between truth and falsehood, because Allah has soldiers that they do not see. Likewise, this address also corrects the group of disbelievers, so that they do not say: "We have our causes, a large number and strong equipment." For the battle between truth and falsehood has occurred before, and truth has triumphed.

The word ﴿fi'ah﴾ (group), when you hear it, conjures up a gathering of people, but it has a particular character: a gathering may exist while each one has his own movement in life. But when we hear the word ﴿fi'ah﴾, it indicates a group with a single movement, engaged in one action. Outside of war, each person has a movement that may differ from the movement of another. But the word ﴿fi'ah﴾ indicates a group of people with one movement in one action for one goal.

Undoubtedly, war depicts this process most precisely; indeed, it is war that unites every group in the single movement, the single action, and the single goal, because each individual of any group cannot protect himself alone. Each one falls back (yafī'u) and returns to the group, and cannot separate himself from his group. But in the movement of ordinary life, the individual can separate himself from his group.

Thus the word ﴿fi'ah﴾ indicates a group of people in a single process, and the word always comes in war to depict each camp facing another. When the Truth says: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met﴾, meaning there is a conflict between two groups, and the Truth clarifies the nature of each group, saying: ﴿one host fighting in the way of Allah, and another, disbelieving﴾. When we examine the Qur'anic text closely, we find that the Truth did not give us a description of the group that fights in the way of Allah, nor did it state that it is a believing group, and it made clear that the other group is disbelieving. This means that the group fighting in the way of Allah must be a believing group. The Truth did not state that the disbelieving group fights in the way of Satan, being satisfied that its disbelief must lead it to fight in the way of Satan.

The Truth has omitted from the description of the first group what is indicated by the description of the second group.

We know the description of the group fighting in the way of Allah from its counterpart in the verse, which is the other group.

So the counterpart of "disbelieving" is "believing." We also know that the disbelieving group fights in the way of Satan merely by our knowing that the first group, the believing one, fights in the way of Allah. In the language this is called ihtibak, which is to omit from the first what is affirmed in the second, and to omit from the second what is affirmed in the first, so as not to repeat the statement, and to clarify the close linkage between fighting in the way of Allah and faith, and fighting in the way of Satan and disbelief.

Thus the verse, in this meaning, makes clear to us the following: there has already been a sign for you, that is, a very wondrous matter that does not proceed and does not agree with the logic of realistic causes, in two groups. When the believing group met the disbelieving group in combat, the believing group, defined by the goal for which it fights—which is fighting in the way of Allah—was able to triumph over the disbelieving group that fights in the way of Satan.

Then the Truth says: ﴿They see them as twice their number with their own eyes﴾. We are faced with two groups: who sees, and who is seen? Who is the seer and who is the seen?
