The sun has never refused to shine on people one day, nor has the wind refused to blow, nor has the sky refused to rain, and the earth has never said to a human: "You disobey God, so I will not make anything grow for you," nor has a person come to ride the subjugated beast only for it to say: "No; you are disobedient, so I will balk and not let you ride my back."

Thus we see that everything other than humans is subjugated and compelled to the purpose desired of it, which is the service of that human. The human alone is the one who has choice. That is why we must always be mindful that God has made for creation both subjugation and direction, and made agreement among all kinds, but division came to humans. So the True One, glory be to Him, said:

﴿Do you not see that to God prostrate whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth, and the sun and the moon and the stars and the mountains and the trees and the creatures, and many among mankind? But many deserve the punishment. And whoever God humiliates, for him there is no honourer. Indeed, God does what He wills.﴾ [al-Hajj: 18]

The prostrating inanimate things subjugated are: "the sun, the moon and the stars"; the prostrating vegetation subjugated is "the trees"; and likewise "the creatures", for they are among the beings over whom the judgment of the Truth applies unanimously, that they all prostrate, humbled and subjugated. As for humans, the Truth said of them: ﴿and many among mankind, and many deserve the punishment﴾.

So where did the division come? It came among humans. Why? Because God created the human to be free to choose. Could God not have created the human subjugated like the rest of creatures? Is subjugation not a proof of the power of the one who subjugates, and that nothing of His creation will escape His power? That is true, but just as the True One wanted to establish power and dominance through subjugation, He wanted to establish love through choice. So whoever is free to believe or disobey, and then chooses to believe, it is through this choice that the human establishes his being beloved to God.

Thus God divided creation into a compelled category that establishes power, and a chosen category that establishes being beloved, and for this reason God willed that the human should be free to act or not to act. So why then does not

Then, after that, the Truth (Allah), glorified is He, says: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah as He should be feared...﴾

Allah has first granted the believers immunity, by their not listening to the words of the enemies of the religion. When we hear the word "Be mindful (ittaqu)," let us understand that there are things that cause you fatigue and harm, so you must place a shield (wiqayah) between yourself and them. For this reason the Truth said:

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 131]

It is the Truth that asks man to place between himself and the Fire a shield (wiqayah) and a veil that protects him from it. And the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, when He says, for example:

﴿And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 4]

That is: make for yourself a veil between you and Allah that protects you from His anger. Someone may say: how can that be, when I, as a believer, want to live in the companionship (ma'iyyah) of Allah?

We say: you make the shield for yourself from the attributes of Allah's majesty (jalal), while you take shelter under the attributes of beauty (jamal). The true believer is the one who makes for himself a shield from the attributes of Allah's majesty, which are subjugation, dominance, and others. Likewise the Fire is among the hosts of the attributes of majesty. So when the Truth says ﴿Fear the Fire﴾ or ﴿Fear Allah﴾, the meaning is one. When a person hears the words of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿Fear Allah as He should be feared﴾, what does "as He should be feared (haqq tuqatihi)" mean? The word "haqq" - as we know - means the thing that is firm, that does not vanish or waver, that is, it does not end and does not fluctuate; this is the truth.

So what is the right of the God-fearing? It is that your faith, O believer, be firm, one that does not leave you and with which you do not waver. Fearing Allah as He should be feared is following His method, so that Allah is obeyed by following the method and is not disobeyed, is remembered and not forgotten, and is thanked and not ungrateful. The path of obedience lies in following the method through "do" and "do not do," and in remembrance without forgetfulness; because the servant may obey Allah and implement the method of Allah, yet the blessings that Allah has created may occupy the servant away from Allah, and the method calls you to remember Him in every blessing He bestows upon you, and beware lest the blessing make you forget the Bestower.

The servant thanks Allah and does not disbelieve in the blessings that Allah has granted him. As long as you, O servant, receive every blessing and return it to Allah, saying: "What Allah wills; there is no power except with Allah," and do not disbelieve in the blessings, that means you render the right of the blessing, and every blessing whose right the servant renders means it is a blessing for which the servant thanks his Lord and has not disbelieved in it.

It has been said regarding the meaning of ﴿as He should be feared﴾: that is, that the blame of no blamer should take you in (the matter of) Allah, or that you speak the truth even against yourself. This is what is called "the right of piety," i.e., the piety of the Truth, which is considered piety in truth and sincerity. The scholars said: when this verse was revealed and the Companions heard it, the Companions felt weak in themselves before its demand, so some of them said: who can achieve the right of piety? It is said that Allah then revealed:

﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [At-Taghabun: 16]

Does this mean that Allah first imposed on people what they cannot bear, and then said afterward: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾? No; indeed the Truth, glorified is He, does not impose except what is within capacity (wus'), and people may misunderstand His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾, so the servant says: I am not able to carry out that obligation, and this servant thinks that the obligation falls from him. No; this is a mistaken understanding. His saying, the Truth: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ means that you fear Allah with what is within your capacity of ability; so whatever you are able to do, you must do. No one should flee to the opposite meaning and say: I am not able; because Allah knows the limits of your ability.

When you are unable, it is He - glorified is He - who lightens (the burden). You do not lighten it for yourself, O servant; the true Creator is the One who knows whether the matter is beyond your ability or not, and when the matter is beyond your ability, it is Allah who lightens it for you. For this reason, man should not use the true saying:

﴿Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 286]

in other than its proper place; because man cannot estimate capacity and then build the obligation upon that capacity. Rather, you must understand, O man, that it is Allah who created the soul, and He who sent down the obligation to suit the capacity of the soul; and since the Creator of the soul is Allah, He is the All-Knowing of the soul's capacity when He prescribed the method for it. It is He, glorified is He, who imposed the obligation, and He knows that the soul has capacity, so He does not charge a soul except with what it can bear. If He, glorified is He, has imposed an obligation, then know, O servant, that He has imposed it within your capacity; and when there happens to a person what is difficult for him or prevents him from performing what he was charged with in full, He - glorified is He - sets out relief for us and sends down concessions for us. An example of that: the sick person or the traveler has the concession of breaking the fast in Ramadan, and the traveler may shorten the prayer.

So Allah, glorified is He, is the One who knows the limits of capacity of the soul He created; therefore you do not first estimate your capacity and then estimate the obligation upon it, but estimate the obligation first, and say: since the Truth has imposed it, it is within capacity. In the concluding part of the noble verse, His saying: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾, we find ourselves before a prohibition of an action, which is: not dying except while the person is a Muslim.

How so? Would anyone say to you: do not die? That matter is not in your choice, because it is a decree that descends upon you. If it is said to you: do not die, you would be astonished, because no one possesses that; but if it is said to you: do not die except while you are Muslim, you reflect, and through reflection you arrive at the conclusion that the forbidden action, "do not die," is not within human power; but the state in which the action occurs, namely "except while you are Muslim," is within human power; so you say to yourself: death comes without any work of mine, but the words "except while you are Muslim" are within my ability, because Islam is by my own choice.

It is true that you do not know when death will befall you; therefore you take precaution, and precaution means that you remain Muslim until death meets you at any moment while you are Muslim.

So, the saying of Allah: ﴿And do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ is a prohibition of the first action, which is not in our choice. The state in which we have choice is ﴿and do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. How do we reconcile the two matters? Death is not in the choice of any of us as to when it befalls him; so we come to the matter in which we have choice, which is that we strive to be Muslims, and each of us remains holding firmly to the handles of Islam, so that if death meets him at any moment, he is a Muslim; as if the Truth, glorified is He, is saying to us: hold fast to your Islam, for you do not know when death will befall you.

And concealing death from man is not ambiguity as some think; no. It is the most complete, far-reaching clarification; because the concealment of death, and its appointed time from man—in time and state, in age and cause—all of that clarifies death most clearly. Why? Because when Allah has reserved the knowledge of death, man is always awaiting death at any moment; and since man is awaiting death at any moment, this is a wide clarification, indeed the widest clarification.

Almighty Allah says after that: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together...﴾

This noble saying came to alert all the believers, through addressing the Aws and the Khazraj, as if He were saying: know that boasting before Islam was about things that have nothing to do with Islam. But when Islam comes, boasting is by Islam alone. So if a person overlooks what came before Islam by saying, "Among us is so-and-so, and among us is so-and-so," the reply comes: No; that was before Islam.

It happened that the Aws said, after Islam, "Among us is Khuzaymah," and one of the Khazraj said, "Among us are Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Zayd ibn Thabit." Then one of the Aws said, "Among us is Handhalah ibn al-Rahib, and this Handhalah is the 'washed by the angels' (ghasil al-mala'ika). And Khuzaymah ibn Thabit is a noble companion whose testimony the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made equal to two testimonies, because Khuzaymah was a man of luminous faith. The luminosity of certainty guided him to the correct judgment."

For the Prophet (ﷺ) had bought a horse from a Bedouin and went to bring the price, but the Bedouin denied the sale, because some people had raised the price of the horse without knowing that the Messenger had bought it. So the Bedouin called out to the Messenger and said: "If you are buying this horse, buy it; otherwise I will sell it."

The Prophet said to the man: "Did I not already buy it from you?" The man said: "Bring a witness who will testify to that." The man had seized the opportunity that the Prophet had bought from him with no one present at that moment. Our master Khuzaymah was sitting there at the moment the man demanded a witness from the Prophet. So our master Khuzaymah said: "I testify, O Messenger of Allah, that you have indeed bought it."

Because the man was a liar, he said to himself: "Perhaps Khuzaymah saw us while I was selling the horse to the Prophet." So the man fell silent and left. After the man had left, the Messenger called Khuzaymah and said to him: "O Khuzaymah, by what do you testify when you were not with us?" He said: "Do I not believe you about the news of heaven, yet not believe you about what you say? I know you say nothing but the truth; we have trusted you in something greater than that, in our religion." The Messenger knew that Khuzaymah possessed the luminosity of affirmation and good inference, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Khuzaymah testifies for, that suffices for him."

So a matter that requires two witnesses is sufficed by the testimony of Khuzaymah. Thereby the Messenger (ﷺ) gave Khuzaymah the distinction and made his testimony equal to the testimony of two men. Let us see how Allah united the Aws and the Khazraj in the compilation of the Qur'an. Zayd ibn Thabit said: "I resolved upon myself not to write any verse unless I found it written and witnessed by two men, except the last verse of al-Tawbah, which I found written but witnessed by no one except Khuzaymah." The Messenger (ﷺ) had said of Khuzaymah: "Whoever Khuzaymah testifies for, that suffices for him." We should know that Zayd ibn Thabit was of the Khazraj and Khuzaymah was of the Aws. Allah united them in the compilation of the Qur'an, so the Awsi and the Khazraji benefited together. This is to show us, Glorified is He, a new indication: that boasting before Islam was about other than Islam, but when Islam comes, any person of any lineage who has done Islam well may take pride in it. So beware, O Awsi, of saying "Among us is Khuzaymah"; the Khazraji too has pride in Khuzaymah. And the Khazraji may not say "Among us is Zayd ibn Thabit," for the Awsi too may take pride in him, because each of them has been joined by Allah to the other in the Qur'an and in Islam. Thus is holding fast to the rope of Allah.

Almighty and Exalted Allah says: ﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah, and do not be divided. And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together﴾. The war had raged between the Aws and the Khazraj for one hundred and twenty years, although the origin of the two tribes is one; they are brothers of the same father and mother. When Islam came, Allah brought their hearts together, and by His favour they became brothers.

This shows us that every sharp movement of a limb must have behind it a stirring and agitation of the heart. The hand does not slap anyone out of emptiness; rather the slap exists in the heart first: ﴿so He brought your hearts together﴾. Allah, Glorified is He, says: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it﴾. The shafa is the edge. Sometimes it is said "shafa" and sometimes "shafah". They were on the edge of the Fire, and whoever is on the edge is about to fall. So it is as if Allah is saying: You were rescued by Islam; and had it not been for Islam, you would have plunged into the Fire.

He, Glorified is He, says: ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may be guided﴾. Thus we see the blessing of Islam in this world: the power of faith to rescue a person from the Fire does not require waiting; rather the believer can see it in this world. The Arabs before Islam were troubled by disputes, divided by tribal fanaticism, and every day in discord. When Islam came they became brothers. This is an immediate blessing in this world, and the world, as we know, is not the abode of recompense; so what then of what will be in the Hereafter, which is the abode of recompense and permanence.

His saying, the Truth: ﴿that you may be guided﴾ is meant to be that you continue upon your guidance. He addressed them: ﴿when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became by His favour brothers﴾. And when the Legislator asks of you what you are upon, know that the Legislator wants you to sustain it. So when the Truth says "O you who believe" — that is, with the faith you already have before my speech — renew your faith after my speech, so that faith may continue for you always.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 104:

Then the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿And let there be among you a community (ummah) who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong...﴾

The word "ummah" is used in several senses. Sometimes it is used to mean a group belonging to a single kind, such as the Arab nation (ummat al-'Arab), the Persian nation (ummat al-Furs), or the Roman nation (ummat al-Rum). Sometimes the word "ummah" is used to mean a religion (millah), that is, a faith (din). A third usage of the word "ummah" is to mean a period of time, as in the saying of the Truth:

﴿And he among the two who had been delivered said, and remembered after a while (ummah): "I will inform you of its interpretation, so send me forth."﴾ [Yusuf: 45]

The man to whom Sayyidna Yusuf interpreted the dream remembered Sayyidna Yusuf after an ummah, that is, after a period of time. And sometimes the word "ummah" is used for a man who combines all the qualities of goodness.

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah, devoutly obedient to Allah, upright, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ [al-Nahl: 120]

This is because the qualities of goodness do not necessarily all gather in one person; they may be gathered among a number of individuals, so that there is one who is distinguished by a good quality, another who is characterized by a different good quality, and a third who has a third good quality. From the whole community the image of perfection appears. But in Ibrahim, peace be upon him, all the qualities of complete goodness were gathered.

When you say to a person, "Let there be from you a brave person," what does that mean? It means that the person should strip himself of his self and bring forth from it a brave person, by training it and accustoming it to that until he becomes brave. Or you say to another, "Let there be from you a generous one," that is, bring forth from yourself a generous man.

And the Truth's saying, glory be to Him: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good﴾.

This statement means that there should be from you, O addressees, a community who invite to good. It also means that you should all be a community who invite to good. Some scholars hold that this statement means: let there be from you a group who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. But there is a deeper understanding than this, namely that this verse commands that the whole community of Muslims be a community who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. That is, this verse demands of the whole community of Muslims that they do so, and it is not restricted to a specific group among them alone to enjoin right and forbid wrong; rather it is obligatory that the entire Muslim community enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. Whoever knows a ruling of the rulings must enjoin it.

Some scholars have said that the one who commits an evil has another ruling as well, which is that he should forbid others from evil. That is, the believing person is obligated to two things: first, not to do evil; second, to forbid evil. Therefore, if advice comes to you from a person forbidding you from evil, while he himself has committed it, do not say to him: "Reform yourself first and follow what you advise," do not say that, lest he say to you what the poet said:

"Take my knowledge and do not rely on my deed;
Gather the fruits and leave the wood for the fire."

But the more fitting course for one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is that he be the first to act upon his own words, so that he does not enter among those about whom Allah said:

﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do.﴾ [al-Saff: 2–3]

So the Truth's saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good﴾ means: strip from yourselves a community gathered together in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Listen to His saying, exalted is He:

﴿By time, indeed mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience.﴾ [al-'Asr: 1–3]

This noble surah clarifies the creed and its aim, which is faith and righteous action. Then the Truth said: "wa-tawasaw" (and advised each other), and did not say "wa-wassaw." What is the meaning of "tawasaw"? It means that every believer should know that he is among those who are weak, and likewise his believing brother; one of them may weaken before a sin and commit it, but the other is not weak before that sin. Therefore it falls to the one who is not weak to counsel the weak one, and it is also necessary for the weak one to be attentive so that he counsels with others. Islam has not made one group to counsel others while another group receives counsel; rather we are all counselors (mūṣin, with a kasra on the ṣād) whenever we find someone weak before a sin, and we are all counseled (mūṣan, with a fatha on the ṣād) when we are weak before a sin. Thus tawasi entails interaction between two sides: sometimes you are the one who counsels, and sometimes you are the one who is counseled. Likewise is mutual counsel to patience.

When a calamity befalls one of the Muslims, his brother comes to make him patient; and likewise if a calamity befalls the Muslim brother, his brother makes him patient. When a Muslim at some time needs to be made patient, he finds among his brothers one who makes him patient. The whole community is thus obligated: ﴿and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾.

In this way we understand the meaning of the Truth's saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong; and those are the successful.﴾ The Truth explains inviting to good as enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

The Truth says: ﴿And those are the successful.﴾ The word ﴿al-muflihun﴾ (the successful) is a word that carries its own proof: the one who is successful (muflih) is the one who has taken the profitable bargain. The word is derived from "falaha al-ard" (he tilled the land). The one who tills the earth, ploughs it, and then sows it finds the fruit coming to him in the end; the Truth has brought a matter of meaning through a sensible image. Then the Truth wants to give us something else, saying: beware lest you think that the hardship that befalls you when you do good will not return to you in ease, or that the loss by which you do good will not return to you in completeness. For example, the man who tilled the land and brought out a "kayla" of wheat and sowed it in it. This man may have a foolish wife who says to him: "We have only four kayls of wheat, so how will you take one kayla to throw into the earth?" This woman does not know that the kayla the husband took is the one that will bring a number of ardabs of wheat.

So beware of understanding that Islam takes anything from you without wanting to give you things.

The farmer who toils with ploughing and irrigation, whose brow is covered with sweat and the dust of the earth, and whose feet sink into the mud and water, you see him on the day of harvest joyful and glad with his crop. As for another who did not toil with ploughing and whose brow was not covered with beads of sweat, he comes on that day sorrowful and regretful. So beware of looking at the burdens of religion as matters that deprive you of benefit; rather they are matters that multiply benefit for you, that is, they increase your gain. And beware of thinking that a ruling of Allah has come to encroach upon your freedom; rather it has come to prevent the aggression of others against you.

We said before: when the Shari'ah obligates every person not to steal anyone's property, it is a restriction for the sake of preserving the wealth of millions, and it is an implicit commitment for all people not to steal anything from this person; and here we find security spreading through faith among everyone.

If you look at what religion has prevented people from practising against you, you would know the value of the obligations of faith. When the obligation commands that no one cast his eyes upon the womenfolk of his neighbour, this obligation is issued to all people so that Allah protects your womenfolk from the eyes of people. The obligation has restricted the freedom of others for your sake, and they are many, and it has restricted your freedom for the sake of others, and you are one.

So we must remember that every obligation gives righteousness and success. The earth takes the grain and gives you seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. So do not look at what the obligation has taken from your freedom, for it has taken for you from the freedoms of others as well. And do not say: "The obligation has reduced my movement for myself," for it will give you more fruits than what it has deprived you of.

And the Truth (Allah) says after that: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after clear proofs had come to them...﴾

This wise statement forbids following desire (hawa), which leads to division. Despite the clarity of the signs of the Truth, Glory be to Him, for those who follow desire after the matter of the truth has become clear, Allah will cast them into the Fire, and for them is a great punishment.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 106:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says: ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black...﴾

Here we must know that blackening and whitening are among the effects of the differences of environments in this world. The person with black skin has been given by God a constitution that differs from that of the white-skinned person in a way that suits his environment, for the pigment material of the skin in his body is present in strength, to give him the color suitable for living with the conditions of his environment. As for the white-skinned person, his body does not possess a sufficient amount of pigment material, because his environment does not need such pigment material.

So blackness in this world is to the benefit of the one who is black. As for this verse, it speaks of what we will see in the Hereafter, where blackness and whiteness will be different, just as the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the heavens into other than the heavens; likewise the matter of blackness and whiteness will be transformed. It will not be blackness or whiteness for the sake of environments. Therefore you will be astonished on the Day of Resurrection, for you may see a person who was black in this world and find him white in the Hereafter, and find another person whose color was white in this world and then became black in the Hereafter.

Let no one suppose that the black person in this world is disliked by God. No, God gives each one what suits him, as evidenced by the fact that God has provided him with the color that strengthens him for the environment in which he lives. In our human sphere, we give the vaccine to any person traveling to some place, so as to protect him from the evil of a disease in the place to which he goes. Likewise, the creation of God on earth: He, glorified is He, has given every human being in his constitution the immunity that protects him. So God does not dislike blackness, because it is a protection for the human being from the environment. This matter will change on the Day of Resurrection, just as the earth will be changed into other than the earth, and the faces of believers will whiten, and the faces of disbelievers will blacken.

Or blackness and whiteness are both a matter of convention (i'tibari), as evidenced by the fact that you see one who is white but whose face has dust upon it, covered by darkness, and you see another who is black in color but the light of certainty fills his face and the radiance of righteousness shines from him, and you cannot prevent your eyes from gazing at him continually. Therefore the Truth says:

﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22-23]

That is, what is within the soul overflows onto the mold of the human being and his features display it. The black-skinned person may have a face shining with cheerfulness, brightness, and manifestation with an enchanting attractiveness, and the white-faced person may be dark of spirit.

Thus we understand that a person's blackness of skin in this world is only to help him adapt to the environment. An example of this is the blackness and whiteness of the eye: can anyone say that the whiteness of the eye is better than its blackness, or the reverse? No; because everything is prepared for its function.

Another example: when a construction worker comes to bend a straight iron column and twist it, is it said that this man has crooked the iron? No; he wants to shape the iron rod so that it is suitable for a specific function. Likewise, blackness or whiteness in this world is what God willed so that it suits the conditions of life in the environment. As for the Hereafter, the world has passed away and perished, and the earth will not be the earth and the heaven will not be the heaven. The Truth says:

﴿On the day when the earth will be changed to other than the earth, and the heavens as well, and they will come forth before God, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ibrahim: 48]

The believer, when he sees what God has prepared for him of enduring bliss, receives God's bounty with an uplifted soul, joy, and delight. As for the one who sees his place in the Fire, his face must be darkened. And the Truth, glorified is He, addresses a question to these people: ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief?﴾ It is as if this is a matter that surprises those who knew these people in this world; for they saw them in this world with white faces, but they see them on the Day of Resurrection with dusty blackness upon their faces and darkness covering them, so they say to them: ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief?﴾ It is as if that is the mark of one who disbelieves after belief. This is their characteristic and their sign in the Hereafter, that is, what has turned you to this color? It is disbelief after belief.

So who are those who disbelieved after belief?

This means that belief preceded and then disbelief came upon belief, and they died upon that disbelief. This is a view that applies to those who apostatized from Islam, such as Ibn al-Ashlat and others; these disbelieved after belief. Or ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief?﴾ makes us say: the "afterness" here must have a "beforeness." Did not God take a covenant from His creatures in the realm of the atoms (alam al-dharr) when He brought them out from the loins of Adam? And He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Am I not your Lord?¨ They said: "Yes"﴾. It is a confession of faith existing in the realm of the atoms; so whoever comes in reality to nullify this matter has disbelieved after belief. Or: "Did you disbelieve after your belief in Muhammad, after the good tidings came to you, which you knew and read in the Torah and the Gospel, and you were certain that he was coming without doubt, and that he is the Messenger of this community and the Seal of the Prophets?" The saying of the Truth applies to you:

﴿And when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it; so the curse of God is upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]

So this statement is either about the apostates, or disbelief in the reality of the world after belief in the realm of the atoms when God took the covenant from all people, or disbelief after belief in the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, whose good tidings came in the Torah and the Gospel, or it is about the people of desires who took the religion and made it into sects, like the groups that departed from Islam while claiming affiliation to it, such as the Baha'is, the Qadianis, and others. The verse admits all of this, and when we reflect upon the Qur'anic text, we find that it encompasses all these meanings.

Here we note that the Truth, glorified is He, mentioned only: ﴿Did you disbelieve after your belief? So taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve.﴾ This is a statement specific to the disbelievers only, who taste the punishment because of disbelief, and this means that the believer, by his belief, will receive the reward of his deeds.

Allah says: ﴿As for those whose faces will turn white, they will be in Allah's mercy, abiding therein forever.﴾

We should always notice that when Allah describes the reward of a believer for his faith and obedience, He sometimes says:

﴿They are the companions of the Garden; therein they will abide forever.﴾ [al-A'raf: 42]

and at other times He says:

﴿As for those who believed in Allah and held fast to Him, He will admit them to mercy from Him and bounty, and guide them to Himself on a straight path.﴾ [al-Nisa': 175]

What is the difference between the two? People in worship are of two types. Some worship Allah and desire the delights of Paradise, so Allah gives them Paradise as a reward for their worship and their righteous deeds. Others worship Allah because Allah deserves to be worshipped, and Paradise does not even cross their minds. These attain the very mercy itself; they attain the meeting with the Face of Allah.

And what is the difference between Paradise and mercy? Paradise is a creation of Allah, so it endures by Allah's keeping it in existence; but mercy endures by the enduring of Allah, and this is a sufficient guarantee. Whoever sees in Allah good worship for His own sake—glorified is He—Allah places him in mercy.

We have said before that there is a Garden among the Gardens called "'Illiyyun," in which there is none of the pleasures we have heard of in Paradise, such as the flesh of birds and other things; there is nothing in it except seeing Allah. And since the servant does not eat out of hunger in the Hereafter, which is better for him: the Garden of pleasures, or the pleasure of seeing the Face of Allah?

Do you enjoy the blessing or the Bestower? There is no dispute that enjoying the sight of the Bestower is more exalted and lofty than enjoying other pleasures. The precise wording of the Qur'an makes clear to us that mercy encompasses these righteous servants and surrounds them; they are within mercy and enter into it, so mercy does not merely touch them but surrounds them, and they abide in it forever. The Truth confirms this with a new locative phrase in His saying: ﴿they will abide therein forever﴾. It is as if there is a mercy into which the servants are admitted, and then He reassures us that it will never be removed from us. So the first "fihā" (in it) is for entering into mercy, and "fī" in the first place indicates entry into mercy, while the second "fīhā" is for abiding forever.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 108:

Then the Truthful, glorified is He, says: ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth...﴾

The verses of Allah are His proofs, His evidences, and His recompenses. Whoever has his face blackened on the Day of Resurrection receives the punishment, and whoever has his face whitened receives the mercy, and he abides in it forever. ﴿These are the verses of Allah, which We recite to you in truth.﴾ So what is it that makes a person not speak the truth? There must be a motive within that person; for truth, when it is followed, guides him, so he speaks other than the truth. But is there anything that wearies the Creator? No. Glorified and exalted is He, far above that and above every deficiency or defect. Therefore He must say only the truth, for nothing lies outside His dominion. He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the worlds.﴾ He negates injustice from Himself, as He said:

﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ [Fussilat: 46]

The Truth does not desire injustice in any way, neither from Himself nor from you, O servants. And how does injustice come about? The manifestations of injustice are, as we know, that you seize a person without a crime; this is injustice. Or that you do not give a person his due measure of goodness; this is injustice. And what does one who commits injustice do? He wants the matter to return to his benefit. If he wants to seize a person without a crime, he does so to satisfy a grudge and rancour in his soul, and he may fabricate a crime against a person because he sees that this person might threaten him in some interest, and he knows his deviation in it, so he imprisons him, for example, or puts him in jail so that he will not expose him.

Thus, a person cannot turn from the truth to injustice except that he wants to achieve a benefit or to ward off harm from himself. And Allah will not achieve for His own Essence a benefit through injustice, nor ward off a harm that comes to Him from His creation; He is far above that, for He is the Subduer above His servants. And the Hadith Qudsi says: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself, and I have made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another."

And the unjust among mankind is ignorant. Why? Because he has strengthened the one he wronged, and has not weakened him; the wrongdoer oppresses so that he may weaken the oppressed before himself. So we say to him: you are foolish, of little intelligence, for you have strengthened him against yourself and done the opposite of what you intend. And let us clarify that, and to Allah belongs the highest example: we are all the dependents of Allah. Let us move to the circle of our daily lives and look at our children. When one of us has children, and one of the children wrongs his brother, the father's heart is with the wronged one, and the father tries to please his wronged son. Thus the wrongdoing child harmed his brother with a harm suited to his childhood, but he gave him a benefit suited to his father's strength; he does not know the reality of how he has strengthened his brother.

And since we are all the dependents of Allah, what does Allah do when He sees, glorified is He, one of His creatures wronging another of His creatures? It must be that the Truth will encompass the wronged one with His care, and thus the wrongdoer strengthens the wronged one. By that, the wrongdoer announces his foolishness. For if he were intelligent, he would not have wronged, and he would have been stingy with his enemy's being wronged, and he would have said: he does not deserve that I wrong him, for through my wronging him Allah will give him a great reward, which is to place him directly in His protection and care.

And we may find someone who wrongs for the sake of immediate gain, and this person forgets that he will never escape from the One who created him. We say to such a person: you will never escape from the One who created you; rather, you have fled from the created being and hidden yourself, and you tried to achieve immediate gain for yourself. But the Creator is the Self-Subsisting, who is not overtaken by drowsiness or sleep. It is as if the Truth, glorified is He, reassures us that we may sleep soundly, for He, glorified is He, is not overtaken by drowsiness or sleep.

﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the worlds.﴾ Because injustice arises only from a desire for benefit without right, or a desire for harm without crime, and Allah is independent of that. Therefore we find that the Truth affirms His independence from creation and that He owns the whole universe, so He says: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 109:

﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned.﴾

He is the Owner of dominion; everything belongs to Him, exists through Him and is under His possession, and every matter is returned to Him. We know that the noble Qur'an was revealed from Allah in multiple recitations (qira'at). In some of them it appears as ﴿تَرْجِعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ with a fatha on the tā' in the active voice (tarji'u), and in another recital as ﴿تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾ with a ḍamma on the tā' in the passive voice (turja'u). Likewise, ﴿ترجعون﴾ also comes with a ḍamma and with a fatha on the tā', and all of them, as we have said, are recitations from Allah.

When the Truth says ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تَرْجِعُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the tā', it means that we return to Him by choice, because the believer loves and desires to reach the Hereafter, since his deeds were good in this world; so he hastens and races toward the Hereafter. At another time He, exalted is He, says ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the tā'. This applies to the disbeliever or the disobedient. Each of them tries not to go to the Other, but the matter is not up to his will; he is compelled to return to the Hereafter. That is why we find the Qur'anic expression:

﴿يَوْمَ يُدَعُّونَ إِلَى نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ دَعًّا﴾ [al-Ṭūr: 13]

There are those who push them into the Fire with a push. In our life, and to Allah belongs the highest example, we find the policeman seizing the criminal by his clothing and pushing him into prison. That is the *da'*. And so the words of the Truth ﴿وَإِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ with a ḍamma on the tā' and a fatha on the jīm mean that he is pushed by an overpowering force to the end. As for the believer who is certain, he hastens to his Hereafter, longing for the face of his Lord.

When you recite ﴿وَإِلَى اللَّهِ تُرْجَعُ الْأُمُورُ﴾, someone may say: when did matters come out from Him so that they return to Him? We say: when Allah created the world, He created it with a subjugating power for the benefit of humankind, and He placed in it things by means of causes. If a person does the cause, he obtains the caused (al-musabbab, with a fatha on the shadda'd bā'). The sun shines on us all, and its light, warmth and heat are, by Allah's command, for the believer and the disbeliever alike; Allah has not commanded it to favour the believer alone with its benefits. The air does not pass over the believer alone, but over the believer and the disbeliever; likewise water. The disbeliever cultivates the land and takes its fruits, and the believer cultivates it likewise.

So in the cosmos there are subjugated things, which human capacity does not enter into, and there are causal things: if you do the cause, the caused will come to you. Allah has placed causes for believer and disbeliever alike. When Allah grants some creatures possession of the causes of creation, He is the Self-Subsisting over all; but in the Hereafter there are no causes and no caused things, and therefore the command belongs to Him alone. Read carefully:

﴿لِّمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ لِلَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ﴾ [Ghāfir: 16]

In this world there are people who, by Allah's will, possess causes, possess slaves, and possess authority, because the world is the world of causes. In the Hereafter there is no room for that. The world began with its causes as a gift from Him, and returned to Him: ﴿لِّمَنِ الْمُلْكُ الْيَوْمَ لِلَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ﴾. To one who takes pride in causality we say: be a captive of causality, if you are able. To one who takes pride in strength, because it is apparently the cause of movement, we say: keep your strength, if you are capable. To one who takes pride in dominion we say: hold on to your dominion, if you are able. No one is capable of keeping anything; everything returns to Allah. Though it may appear that some things are yours now, on the Day of the Hereafter every matter belongs to Allah, and everything returns to Him: He began it, and to Him it returns.

Allah then says: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong...﴾

This goodness has attributes and components: ﴿you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in Allah﴾. If one of these components is missing, the goodness is dissolved from you. The goodness that belongs to you rests on three things: enjoining what is right (amr bil-ma'ruf), forbidding what is wrong (nahy 'an al-munkar), and belief in Allah (iman billah).

When you hear the words "ma'ruf" (what is right) and "munkar" (what is wrong), you find that the word is coined for its correct meaning. "Ma'ruf" is what people recognize and take pride in, and what every person is glad to have others know about him. "Munkar" is what people reject and feel ashamed of. Thus every person loves that the signs of goodness be known of him by others, while every person rejects the signs of evil.

The signs of goodness are beloved and praised even by the deviant. The thief himself, when he is in a gathering where no one knows him and he hears that so-and-so has stolen, declares his disapproval of the thief's deed. It is a reprehensible matter, even though he himself commits it. Thus you know that "ma'ruf" and "munkar" are subject to the judgment of the fitrah (innate human disposition). The sound fitrah recognizes good matters and makes them familiar among people, and the sound fitrah rejects reprehensible matters, even from those who commit them.

Allah mentions the matter of belief in Allah after enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Why? Because it is possible for a person to have qualities of generosity and humanity, to enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, do good, give charity, and establish institutions caring for the needy and the helpless, whether health-related or economic, yet he does this from the standpoint of his own human self, not from the standpoint of Allah's method. So all that he does is worthless, and nothing is credited to him, because he did not do it within the framework of belief in Allah. Therefore do not think that one who does good without belief in Allah will be rewarded. Allah rewards those who were upon belief in Him, and [it is required] that Allah be in the mind of the servant at the moment he does good. Whoever does good for the sake of chivalry, humanity, rank, position, or reputation, he receives his reward from those for whom he did it. And since he did it so that it would be said of him, then it has been said. This is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained when he said: "The first of people to be judged on the Day of Resurrection will be a man who was martyred. He will be brought forward and Allah will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. Allah will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I fought for You until I was martyred.' Allah will say: 'You lie. You fought so that it would be said, "He is brave," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, dragged on his face, and thrown into the Fire. And a man who learned knowledge, taught it, and recited the Qur'an, will be brought forward, and Allah will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. Allah will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I learned knowledge, taught it, and recited the Qur'an for You.' Allah will say: 'You lie. You learned knowledge so that it would be said, "He is a scholar," and you recited the Qur'an so that it would be said, "He is a reciter," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, dragged on his face, and thrown into the Fire. And a man whom Allah granted abundance and gave every kind of wealth, will be brought forward, and Allah will make him recognize His blessings, and he will recognize them. Allah will say: 'What did you do with them?' He will say: 'I left no path in which You love spending except that I spent in it.' Allah will say: 'You lie. You did it so that it would be said, "He is generous," and it has been said.' Then he will be ordered, dragged on his face, and then thrown into the Fire."

He receives the reward of his deed from people's words, but Allah rewards in the Hereafter the one in whose mind Allah was when he did the deed. Therefore Allah, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah, does righteous deeds, and says, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"?﴾ [Fussilat: 33]

The believer does righteous deeds and declares that he does them because he is a Muslim. He does not do good because he is a communist, an existentialist, a humanist, and so on. Whatever good a person does, if he abandons acknowledgment of Allah, the treachery of disbelief corrupts every deed, because he has denied and rejected his Creator and disbelieved in Him. Whoever does good for someone should seek the reward of that deed from that someone.

Here, in this verse, there is enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and belief in Allah. But what makes them not believe in Allah even if they do what is right? It is their greed for false position. When Islam came, the people of position in the other religions thought that Islam would strip them of their status, authority, standing, and the benefits they had been obtaining. Some of them foolishly sold the Paradise of this world and feared for their position, status, and benefits, and this was because of lack of discernment. Allah says:

﴿If the People of the Scripture had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110]

Had they believed, their status and authority would have remained for them in the light of belief in Allah, with no trading in religion. They would have received their reward twice: a reward in this world and a reward in the Hereafter, or a reward for their belief in their prophet and another reward for their belief in the Messenger of Allah. But does this statement mean that the People of the Scripture did not believe at all? No. Some of them did believe. Allah, glorified and exalted, gives a true account of them, saying: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾ It would have been expected that the description of some of them be belief, and that the others of their community be disbelievers, since belief is opposed by disbelief. But Allah defines the meaning appropriate to their conduct, saying: ﴿but most of them are defiantly disobedient.﴾

Allah, glorified and exalted, speaks, and states every word with utmost precision. There is a difference between disbelieving while lacking the preliminaries and proofs of faith, and disbelieving while knowing those preliminaries, such as reading the Torah and the Gospel.

The People of the Scripture read the Torah and the Gospel, saw the clear signs, and recognized the good tidings. Therefore, when they disbelieved in the Messenger of Allah, they also transgressed in addition to disbelief. Those among the People of the Scripture who disbelieved in the Messenger of Allah are defiantly disobedient even in their disbelief, because the requirement of their knowledge of the good tidings and signs was that they proclaim belief in the message of the Messenger of Allah. So one of them is not an ordinary disbeliever; rather he is defiantly disobedient even in disbelief, because he knew the truth, then went out from it and transgressed against it.

Since Allah has said: ﴿Among them are believers, but most of them are defiantly disobedient,﴾ what then does the believer among them do with the defiantly disobedient? The defiantly disobedient, who are the majority in Judaism and Christianity, will lie in wait for the believing minority to inflict harm and injury upon them,

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 111:

And the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance. And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾

But the Truth, glory be to Him, reassures this minority against harm from the majority, saying: ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance.﴾ That is: O you minority among the People of the Book who have believed—like ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, who embraced Islam and left Judaism—beware lest you think that the corrupt majority is able to bring punishment upon you. Allah, glory be to Him, declares that the majority's attempt to inflict harm upon the minority of them who have believed will not go beyond mere annoyance.

What is harm (ḍarar), and what is annoyance (adhā)?

Annoyance (adhā) is an event that hurts at the moment it occurs and then ends. Harm (ḍarar), however, is an annoyance that hurts at the time it occurs and has effects after it. When a person slaps another person with a light slap, the light slap hurts, and its pain goes away immediately. But if the slap is strong and causes bruising and swelling, this is harm. So annoyance hurts only for the hour in which the act is carried out, and annoyance may be by word, such as mockery. The corrupt person may mock the one who believes, uttering a word of disbelief or wickedness; that word does no harm to the believer's own self, but it hurts his hearing. The Truth, glory be to Him, reassures the believers that the people of disbelief will not harm them except with annoyance, and this is the utmost of what they can do, and this annoyance leaves no lasting effect.

So the words ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance﴾ mean that they will never be able to inflict anything upon you, except mockery, or slander and insinuation, or a gesture that wounds the feelings of the believer, or glorifying disbelief and exalting it, or uttering a word of immorality or depravity to which the religion does not consent. This is the utmost that the people of corruption can do, and they do not possess harm against the people of faith. Then we see that the reality of the matter has proceeded in this manner with the Muhammadan call and with the soldiers of our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Allah released this word, ﴿They will not harm you, except for some annoyance﴾, and it became a law. Battles took place between the soldiers of the Messenger of Allah and the people of corruption, and it was established that the people of corruption were unable to inflict harm on the people of faith beyond annoyance.

Let us look at what happened to Banu Qaynuqa, what happened to Banu Qurayza, what happened to Banu al-Nadir, and what happened to the Jews of Khaybar. Did they harm the believers except with annoyance? They said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Do not be deceived, O Muhammad, that you met a people who were inexperienced and had no knowledge of war, and so you prevailed over them. If you fight us, you will know who the men are." That was merely talk with the tongue.

History carries to us what happened to them all: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) defeated them. After this, they wanted to rise from annoyance to real harm, but Allah did not enable them, because the Truth says: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped.﴾ So if the people of corruption wish to escalate annoyance against the believers in order to inflict real harm, the disbelievers will turn their backs before the believers, and their defeat is something unavoidable.

In the language we know what we call the "conditional" (al-sharṭ) and what we call the "response" (al-jawāb). ﴿In﴾ (in) is a conditional particle that apocopates the conditional verb and its response. If the verb is one of the "five verbs" (al-afʿāl al-khamsa), we delete the nūn, and therefore we find the true saying: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾.

﴿They fight you﴾ (yuqātilūkum) is the conditional verb, from which the nūn has been deleted. ﴿They turn to you their backs﴾ (yuwallūkumu al-adbār) is originally yuwallūnakum al-adbār, and it is the response of the condition, from which the nūn has been deleted. When the conjunction comes after that, should it be in the nominative (rafʿ) or the apocopate (jazm)? The custom is that the conjunction is in the apocopate (jazm)! But the Truth conjoins in the nominative (rafʿ), so there comes His saying: ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ (thumma lā yunṣarūn). This is an irregular i'rab vowel that makes the Arab mind turn its attention to the fact that there is a great matter, because the speaker is Allah, glory be to Him. How did the nūn come?

Here we pause, and let us pronounce the verse as human speech: "If they fight you, they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped." This statement would be a record of a single battle. But what will happen after that? What happens when the believers fight the people of disbelief and corruption? The answer is: ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. This wise statement carries a matter far from condition and consequence; it is a judgment from Allah upon the people of corruption that they will never be helped, whether they fight or do not fight. It is a fixed, separate matter, not conjoined to the condition. The cause of non-victory is not the fighting, but the disbelief.

If we examine the meaning closely, letter by letter, after having examined it sentence by sentence, we would find a new meaning. One might suppose the statement should have been phrased differently, as "they will turn their backs to you, so they will not be helped," because what comes after the fāʾ (fa) indicates that they will not be victorious over you at the start of your encounter, and this is what fa conveys, since it marks sequence and immediate succession. But the Truth brought the particle "thumma" (then), which conveys delay, and this means that they will not be victorious over you, O believers, even if they prepare after a period for a battle to avenge their turning of their backs. It is a judgment of perpetuity, because "thumma" comes for succession with delay, while "fa" comes for immediate succession without delay. Therefore, when we read the Qur'an, we find the use of fa as follows:

﴿Then He caused him to die and buried him﴾ [ʿAbasa: 21]

because entering the grave occurs directly after death. And after that the Truth says:

﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him again﴾ [ʿAbasa: 22]

So if there is a succession after a span of time, the Truth uses "thumma," and if there is an immediate succession without a span, the Truth uses "fa." The succession in the verse we are treating comes after "thumma," as if this were a continuous judgment from the Truth that the people of corruption will not be victorious over the people of faith, even after the present battle between them has ended. It is a defeat by a final judgment. This is the decisive word: ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, and it is more forceful than if it had come as "they will not be victorious." Why? Because it is possible that the people of disbelief would not be victorious by their own selves, but the clarification affirms that they, the people of disbelief, are not victorious neither by themselves, nor are they helped by others either.

﴿Then they will not be helped﴾ is a permanent matter; the matter is not confined to the era of the Messenger of Allah only, but it will remain until the end of time.

It is superficial understanding to say that the verse should have required the phrasing "thumma lā yunṣarū," because the grammar would demand that. But the meaning appropriate to the Speaker, who is the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, who gives assurance and tranquility to the Muslim community before its adversaries, must say: ﴿then they will not be helped﴾, which is more precise even than "they will not be victorious," because "they will be victorious" involves the agency of their own causes, whereas ﴿then they will not be helped﴾ means that there is no victory for them ever, even if some other people take up the cause of the people of corruption and try to help them, they will not be able to do so.

So if you see, O Muslims, a victory of the disbelievers over you from them, or through some people's partisanship on their behalf, know that you have entered with them upon other than the method of Allah. And a person may come and say: How can the Jews triumph over us when we are Muslims? We would say: Do we now follow the method and spirit of Islam? What do we have of Islam and of faith? Do you count yourself as belonging to your Lord during your defeat? And did you enter your battle as an Islamic battle?

No, we have paid attention to everything except Islam. We have given precedence to allegiance to tribalism, nationalism, and ethnicity over faith, so how can we seek victory from Allah? We have no right to seek the help of Allah unless we enter the battle as soldiers of Allah. Defeat occurs when we are not soldiers of Allah, because Allah has guaranteed victory and triumph to His soldiers, saying:

﴿And indeed Our soldiers, they are the victorious﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 173]

So if we are not victorious, be assured that we are not among the soldiers of Allah.

The Exalted says after that: ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found, except under a covenant from God and a covenant from people.﴾

We use the word "ḍaraba" (ضرب) in connection with coins. When we say "this pound was struck (ḍuriba) in Egypt," the meaning is that the craftsman makes a mould from a material harder than the metal from which the currency is made. He carves into it the engravings that bring out the writing and the images on both faces of the pound. Then he pours the material into that mould, and it yields to the mould, so the writing and the images stand out. The material does not resist the mould. It is as if "ḍuriba" means "ulzima" (was compelled), in the passive form in both cases. It is as if the material that is made is bound to the mould into which it is poured, does not resist it, and can take its shape only through it.

So "ḍarb" means compulsion and forcing into an act. When the Exalted says ﴿humiliation has been stamped upon them﴾, it means that humiliation has become binding on them, and they cannot ever be released from it, just as the metal struck as a coin cannot be separated from the mould on which it was minted. It is as if humiliation were a dome struck over them and a mould for them. The Exalted's words ﴿wherever they are found﴾ indicate that they are humiliated wherever they are, in any place. But there is an exception to this. What is it?

It is the Exalted's words ﴿except under a covenant from God and a covenant from people﴾. They do not suffer humiliation when there is a covenant from God, or a covenant from powerful people who provide them with protection. When they were under the covenant of God first, and the covenant of His Messenger, at the moment the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered Medina and granted them a covenant, they were secure. When they betrayed the covenant and did not fulfil it, what happened? Humiliation was stamped upon them again.

So they were secure under the covenant of God, but they betrayed the covenant, and the cord of God was cut off from them. They stirred up the commotion that we know of, and what befell them befell them. This happened to the Banu Qaynuqa, the Banu al-Nadir, the Banu Qurayza and the Jews of Khaybar.

So before that, they were in a covenant with God. You know that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) first arrived in Medina, he built the mosque and concluded a covenant between himself and the Jews, and they lived in tranquillity until they betrayed the covenant, and humiliation was stamped upon them. They were expelled from Medina, as the Exalted says: ﴿Humiliation has been stamped upon them wherever they are found, except under a covenant from God and a covenant from people﴾.

They took the covenant from God through the one who holds authority over people. The Messenger, during his covenant, was in charge of the affairs of the Muslims. Likewise, the situation with them is under those who are in charge of the affairs of Islam, and this happens when affairs proceed according to the method of Islam.

As for the "cord of people," that is because they do not possess any self-generated honour. They are always in humiliation unless they seek honour from a covenant and cord from God, or from the protection of people. We see them in this state in our contemporary life. They must live under the protection of someone. Therefore, when we fought "Israel" in the October War, we were victorious over them until America intervened with its military weight.

The head of the Egyptian state said: "I have no capacity to fight America."

So if the war were only between us and them, their strength would not have lasted. They have no self-generated honour, and they would have honour only if they were under a cord from God or a cord from people. The Exalted, may He be glorified, says of them after that: ﴿They returned with wrath from God, and poverty was stamped upon them﴾. We should notice that humiliation has an exception: they attain honour if they are beside a cord from God or a cord from people. But as for poverty (maskanah), there is no exception to it. The Exalted has said about them in another place in the Noble Qur'an:

﴿Humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with wrath from God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]

Because poverty is an inherent matter in the soul. They are poor by a decree from God. As for humiliation, someone may come to them who helps them and stands by their side. Humiliation is a matter from outside, whereas poverty is in their very selfhood. When poverty is inherent, there is no rescue from it, because no cord from God comes to them to save them from it, and no cord from people protects them from its effects. The Exalted says: ﴿and they returned with wrath from God﴾. Has any of us seen a greater wrath than that God has scattered them across the earth? Let us read the saying of God:

﴿And We divided them into communities upon the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 168]

The only place that sheltered them in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was Yathrib in the Arabian Peninsula. They settled there for a while, and they had scholarly leadership, because they were People of the Book, and economic leadership, and likewise military leadership. This place that sheltered them from dispersal across the earth is the very place they rebelled against. The reason they came to Yathrib was what they found written in their Torah. In the Torah there is something indicating that a prophet would come in this place, and they must follow him, in accordance with the covenant that we mentioned earlier:

﴿And when God took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said: "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that condition?" They said: "We affirm it." He said: "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81]

This covenant requires that the messengers convey the message to the nations to whom they were sent, and that the believers who come after them be informed that there is a Messenger coming from God with the complete method. The Jews came to Yathrib only in hope of welcoming the awaited Prophet so that they would believe in him, and thereafter would become a force against those who disbelieve in God. But what happened? He, may He be glorified, informs us of what they did in His saying:

﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]

So what came after they returned with wrath from God, and after God had sealed their mould with poverty? What is the reason? The answer from the Exalted: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in the signs of God and killed the prophets without right﴾. God sent them wondrous signs, but they disbelieved in them. Those are the signs mentioned in His saying:

﴿And We shaded you with clouds and sent down upon you manna and quail: "Eat of the good things We have provided for you."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 57]

God sent many signs to the Children of Israel. Among them is what came in His saying:

﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Hold firmly to what We have given you, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63]

But they turned away from faith, while before them was Moses (peace be upon him) striking the rock with his staff, from which gushed forth springs of water for them to drink.

﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: "Strike the rock with your staff." There gushed forth from it twelve springs; every people knew their drinking place.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60]

Despite that, they killed the prophets without right. They lied against their prophets and killed them. Concerning them the Exalted says: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. Disobedience was the cause for humiliation to be stamped upon them, for them to return with wrath from God, and for poverty to be stamped upon them, and all of that arose from their own deeds. There is a difference between God initiating an action against them and God punishing them for an action. To understand that, let us read His saying:

﴿For the wrongdoing of those who judaised, We forbade them certain good things that had been lawful for them, and for their turning many away from the way of God﴾ [al-Nisa': 160]

God forbade them good things because of their own wrongdoing against themselves. The meaning of forbidding good things is that God deprived them of a pleasure that is good, because they had taken lawful a pleasure that was not good. The intentions of the Lawgiver run contrary to the intentions of those who deviate from the command of the Lawgiver. As we said before: the Exalted, may He be glorified and exalted, records the truth and the reality, and does not address them all with a single account that encompasses them all. Among them were people who were inclined to believe in the Messenger and in the Qur'an, and some of them actually believed. Therefore, it was part of God's justice to distinguish between those who were considering faith and those who insisted on disbelief.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 113:

Therefore the Almighty says: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah during the night hours while they prostrate.﴾

This is indeed what happened. But which verses of Allah were they reciting? They are the verses that are muhayman (the guardian, dominant ones), the verses of the Qur'an. And why does the Truth say: ﴿while they prostrate﴾? Is there a recitation of the Qur'an at the time of prostration? To understand this explanation, we must know that the Jews do not pray the ʿatama, meaning the prayer at night. So that Allah might give them the Islamic mark, He said of them: ﴿they prostrate﴾, and He described them as performing the ʿatama prayer, which is the 'ishaʾ (night prayer), the prayer of the Muslims. Since they pray the prayers of the Muslims and prostrate, then they are Muslims; or we understand from His saying ﴿while they prostrate﴾ that prayer is the sign of submission, and prostration is the strongest mark of submission in prayer. As long as they pray, they must be reciting the verses of Allah during the hours of the night while performing the prayer with complete humility. We know that among the excellences of worship in Islam, and among the known sunan, is the recitation of the Qur'an at night and the tahajjud prayer, and these are among the stages of the faith-process by which a person enters the station of ihsan (excellence).

And ﴿ānāʾa﴾ is the plural of "inan" (إني), just as "amʿāʾ" (أمعاء) is the plural of "miʿan" (معي). And "ānāʾa" is the collection of times in the night, and not the singular "inan". There is a believer who recites the Qur'an at one time of the night, and another believer who recites the Qur'an at another time, and it is as if the believers spend the night in reciting the Qur'an. Whoever enters with his Lord into the station of ihsan does not pray only the ʿatama prayer, which will take one "inan", meaning one time; but when he prays during the hours of the night, that is evidence that he repeats the prayer and adds to what is obligatory upon him. Since he has added to what is obligatory, he is not satisfied with reciting the Qur'an, because he wants to enter the station of ihsan. That is, he has found his Lord worthy of being prayed to more than what was prescribed for him, as if he says to himself: "You, O Lord, have obligated me with five prayers, but You, O Lord, deserve more than that." It is as if this group of the People of the Book were not content with merely declaring faith in Islam, but entered with their full weight, and prayed during the hours of the night. They loved that the saying of Allah the Exalted should apply to them:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be among gardens and springs, taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that doers of good.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 15-16]

What is the meaning of "muhsin" (doer of good)? It is a description of the person who believed in his Lord and worshipped Allah more than what was obligatory. For example, we were obligated by Allah to pray five prayers, and he adds to them so that they reach twenty, for instance. We were obligated by Allah to fast one month in the year, and some of us fast a number of days in every month. We were obligated to pay zakat at the nisab, and some of us give more than the nisab. He, glorified is He, obligated us to perform Hajj once, and some of us increase the number of times they perform Hajj. So when the servant wants to enter the station of ihsan, his gate is to perform acts of worship of the same kind as what Allah has obligated him with; the servant does not invent or propose the worship by which he worships Allah, but he adds to what Allah has prescribed.

And these people among the People of the Book who believed in Allah, of whom the Qur'an speaks, had entered Islam with their full weight, so they prayed during the hours of the night, recited the Qur'an, entered the station of ihsan, and wanted to apply the saying of the Truth:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 17]

That is, since they prayed during the night and slept only a little, they must have performed the prayer during many hours of the night. When we enter the station of ihsan and pray at night, and stand exposed to the sky with nothing separating us from it, and we look and find bright stars beneath the lowest heaven, and the people of the heavens look at the earth and find, as we find, bright shining stars on the earth, and they ask about them, it is said to them: "They are the houses whose people pray during the hours of the night while prostrating," and every house in which this takes place shines like stars for the people of the heavens. And the Truth adds to the attributes of these people: ﴿and at the dawns they seek forgiveness﴾. Has Allah obligated His creation to pray during the hours of the night, so that they sleep only a little of the night? No, but whoever wants to enter the station of ihsan does this. As for the ordinary Muslim, he is content with the ʿishaʾ prayer, and when dawn comes he performs the obligatory prayer. But whoever enters the station of ihsan sleeps only a little of the night. And the saying of the Truth applies to him:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be among gardens and springs, taking what their Lord has given them. Indeed, they were before that doers of good. They used to sleep but little of the night. And at the dawns they seek forgiveness. And in their wealth there was a right for the beggar and the deprived.﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 15-19]

This is the precision of the Qur'anic exposition that clarifies the station of ihsan, so that in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived, and there is no fixed measure for the wealth that is given out, because the station here is the station of ihsan, which rises above the station of iman. And the station of iman, as we know, has been mentioned in His saying, the Truth:

﴿And those in whose wealth is a known right, for the beggar and the deprived, and those who affirm the Day of Judgment.﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 24-26]

So the person in the station of iman may restrict what he gives from his wealth to the limits of zakat or slightly above it, but in the station of ihsan there is no limit to what is given from wealth. Thus we know that the People of the Book are not all alike; among them are those who entered Islam through the gate of ihsan, of whom the Truth said: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of Allah during the night hours while they prostrate﴾, as if the Truth, by this clear exception, is affirming for us that we should not suppose that all the People of the Book are those of whom He said: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in the verses of Allah and killed the prophets without right; that is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. No; the People of the Book are not all alike, and therefore Allah's judgment does not apply to all of them. Among the People of the Book there is a group standing in recitation of the Qur'an during the night hours while prostrating; they are an upright community. The word "qa'im" (upright, standing) is the opposite of "qa'id" (seated), and qu'ud (sitting/remaining) is not the same as julus (sitting up). Julus is rising from lying down, so it is said: "He was lying down, then sat up."

But when we say "kana qa'iman" (he was standing), we then say "fa-qa'ada" (then he sat), since qu'ud comes after standing. Qu'ud in prayer is comfortable, whereas standing is not comfortable. We know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand in prayer until his feet swelled, because all the weight is on the two feet; but when we sit, we distribute the weight over many parts of the body. When the Truth describes them: ﴿an upright community among the People of the Book﴾, this means that they took on the trust of performing the obligations with complete sincerity, and they performed the prayer with constancy and humility.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah Al-Imran, verse 114

The Truth (al-Haqq) continues describing them in the next verse: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong...﴾

They, in their belief in Allah and the Last Day, and in enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, possess the qualities that Allah has attributed to the best nation brought forth for mankind, which is the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). Some of the People of the Book entered, with their full weight and from the very beginning, the station of ihsan (excellence in conduct).
