Since they had entered the station of ihsan, they were truly anticipating the appearance of the new Prophet. As soon as the new Prophet came, they seized the thread, believed in his message, and became among the best nation brought forth for mankind. Allah, glorified is He, completes their qualities with His saying: ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾. This is like His, glorified and exalted is He, saying concerning the believers:

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Garden whose width is like the width of the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al-Imran: 133]

We know that there is a difference between "speed" (al-sur'ah) and "haste" (al-'ajalah). Speed and haste meet in shortening the time taken for an event. For example, a person covers a distance from one place to another in a given time; the one who hastens in covering the distance is the one who spends the least possible time. But there is a difference between speed and haste, and the first point of difference appears in their opposites. The opposite of speed is slowness, so one says: "So-and-so was quick, and so-and-so was slow." The opposite of "haste" is "deliberation" (al-anah), so one says: "So-and-so took his time in making the decision." Speed is praiseworthy, and its opposite, slowness, is blameworthy; haste is blameworthy, and its opposite, deliberation, is praiseworthy. This is because speed is advancing in what ought to be advanced in, and haste is advancing in what ought not to be advanced in. That is why it is said in proverbs: "In haste is regret, and in deliberation is safety." And the Truth says:

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al-Imran: 133]

Here He, glorified is He, says ﴿and they hasten to good deeds﴾, meaning: whenever a glimmer of good appears to them, they hasten toward it. That is, they advance in what ought to be advanced in. They know that hastening to good is an event, and every event requires movement, movement requires a mover, and a mover implies life. So what guarantees for a person that life will remain his? Therefore, one must hasten to good deeds. Our master ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, may Allah be pleased with him, used to take a midday nap, and his chamberlain would prevent people from waking the caliph. Then the son of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz came and said to the chamberlain:

"I want to enter upon the Commander of the Believers right now." The chamberlain prevented him, saying: "It is an hour in which he rests, and he rests from night or day only at this time, so leave him to rest." Our master ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz heard the commotion and asked the chamberlain. The chamberlain said: "It is your son, and he wants to enter upon you, and I have been insisting that he not enter until you have rested." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said to the chamberlain: "Let him enter." When the son entered upon his father, the son said: "O my father, it has reached me that you are going to give away such-and-such an estate to be endowed in the way of Allah."

ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz said: "I will do so, God willing. Tomorrow we will finalize it." The son asked, questioning: "Will Allah keep you alive until tomorrow?" ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz, weeping, said: "Praise be to Allah who has made among my children one who helps me toward good."

The son wanted his father to hasten to good. As long as the breeze of goodness has blown upon a person, he must seize it, because a person does not know the changes of events within himself. Therefore he must hasten to seize the gift of goodness. Here is the son of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz helping his father toward good. But in our time we may find children who ask to have their father placed under restraint if the father thinks of doing good, forgetting the saying of the Truth: ﴿and they hasten to good deeds, and those are among the righteous﴾.

Here a question arises: for what deed are they righteous?

The answer requires a little reflection. We say in our lives: "So-and-so is a righteous man" (rajul salih), and its opposite is "a corrupt man" (rajul talih). Man is fit for khilafah (vicegerency), for Allah made Adam and his offspring vicegerents on earth. The righteous man sees the good thing in its essence and leaves it as it is or increases its goodness. But the corrupt or mischievous man comes to the good thing and corrupts it, and does no good.

For example, a man may find a well from which people draw water. If he is not a man of resolve, he leaves it as it is. If he is corrupt, he may fill the well with earth. But if the man is one of goodness and resolve, he tries to be creative in serving the people who draw from the well: he thinks about building a high tank, drawing water from the well by a lifting machine, running pipes from the tank to the houses, so that people take water while in their homes. This man has used his mind to increase the goodness of the well.

So the phrase "righteous man" means that he is fit to be a vicegerent on earth and fit to develop the earth, that is, to make it prosperous. He leaves what is good in its essence or increases its goodness, and he tries to set right any matter that is not good. When the righteous man acts, he tries to make his action rest on deep knowledge, and he does not undertake an action that gives superficial benefit and then causes harm afterward.

An example of this is when they invented insecticides; they thought they had overcome crop pests, but they did not know that they had harmed agriculture and the environment more than they had benefited them. So they came back saying: do not use these insecticides, for they have grave harms. Therefore every work must rest on sound scientific foundations. Let us read the saying of the Most High:

﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of those one will be questioned﴾ [Al-Isra: 36], and His saying, glorified is He:

﴿Say: Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the worldly life while they think they are doing well in work﴾ [Al-Kahf: 103-104]

Thus Allah has honored those among the People of the Book who believed, describing them with the true description: they recite the verses of Allah in the hours of the night while prostrating, they believe in Allah and the Last Day, they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and they hasten to good deeds. Then the Truth passes a general judgment on them that they are among the righteous, fit for the building of the universe and for vicegerency on earth.

Afterwards, the Truth adds: ﴿And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them; and Allah is Knower of the God-fearing﴾.

He, glory be to Him, gives them just recompense. Indeed, nothing is lost with Him, and He is the Truth. The good that they do will not be denied to them or concealed from people, because He, glory be to Him, is Knower of the God-fearing. It is possible for a person to perform deeds that no one sees, but the Truth sees every deed, and He is the One who possesses the best recompense. Then the Truth returns to show the state of those who disbelieve, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them anything against Allah...﴾

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 3, verse 116:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will not avail them at all against Allah. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

The disbelievers think that wealth and children may avail them against Allah. They do not estimate correctly. Wealth and children are indeed among the sources of trial (fitnah), in confirmation of the words of the Exalted:

﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.﴾ [al-Anfal: 28]

Since wealth and children are a trial, we must understand the matter as it truly is. Fitnah is not blameworty in itself, because its meaning is test and examination. A person may pass through a trial and succeed in it, such as one who has wealth and children, which are indeed a trial, yet wealth does not deceive him, rather he uses it in good, and his children do not make him proud, rather he teaches them to carry the method of Allah and raises them upon the exemplary conduct of the religion. Therefore, whenever a person hears of any matter containing fitnah, he should not think it is something evil; rather he should remember that fitnah is a test, a trial and an examination, and a person must succeed through this fitnah, for fitnah harms only the one who fails and weakens when confronted with it. The disbelievers do not succeed in the trial of wealth and children; rather a day will come when they will not possess this wealth, nor those children, and even if they possess wealth, they will not buy with it anything in the Hereafter, and each one of their children will be occupied with himself, in confirmation of the saying of the Truth:

﴿O mankind, fear your Lord and dread a day when no father will avail his son at all, nor will a son avail his father at all. Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life delude you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah.﴾ [Luqman: 33]

Every person on the Day of Resurrection has a matter that occupies him away from others, while the disbelievers in this world are occupied with their wealth and children. When we reflect on His saying ﴿will not avail them﴾, we find that we say: "He made him independent of such-and-such" (aghnahu 'an kadha), meaning he made him self-sufficient. So who then is the Rich (al-Ghani)? The Rich is one who has an inherent self that does not need others; if he is hungry, he does not eat from the hand of another. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Richness is not having abundance of goods, but richness is contentment of the soul."

By "al-'arad" (worldly goods) is meant the enjoyment of the worldly life, whether little or much. The enjoyment and goods of this world are like salt water: the more you drink of it, the thirstier you become. The disbeliever among these deceives and cheats himself, and is deluded by wealth and children, forgetting that life proceeds by the command of the One who owns the entire dominion. The disbeliever takes the matter of life out of its proper place. Being deluded by wealth and children in life is a deceptive matter; a person can live life without wealth or children. Whoever is deluded by wealth or children in life will come on the Day of Resurrection and find his wealth and children a cause of regret for him. Why? Because whenever he remembers that wealth and children kept him away from what would qualify him for this situation, he suffers grief and falls into regret.

The Truth, glorified is He, says about this one deluded by wealth and children, while he is a disbeliever in Allah: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ This is a fate fitting for one who falls into the deception of his own self through wealth or children.

How can a person be a companion of the Fire? Let us first know the meaning of the word "companion" (sahib). The companion is the one who is constantly attached; we say: "So-and-so is the companion of so-and-so," meaning he is attached to him. But from where does companionship begin? It is the first "so-and-so" who initiates the companionship, and the second "so-and-so" who either accepts or rejects it. This is a matter we may or may not know. Regarding companionship with the Fire, we see that a person blames himself and reproaches himself for having chosen the Fire and befriended it.

Do we not see in life a person who has committed a sin and suffered harm, so he strikes himself and says: "I am the one who deserves what has befallen me and merits it"? Likewise the disbelieving person finds himself on the Day of Resurrection, entering the Fire, and says to himself: "I deserve what I have done to myself." And the Fire will say at that moment, in response to the question of the Truth to it:

﴿On the Day We will say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it will say, "Are there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30]

In the Hereafter we see the parts of the disbelieving person hating their owner. If a person has authority over his parts in this world, which are subject to his will, those parts will come on the Day of Resurrection while their owner is subject to their will. The wrongdoer says to his hand in this world, "Strike so-and-so and strengthen the slap," and his hand does not disobey him in this world, because Allah created it subject to his will. And the one who wrongs himself through disbelief commands his tongue to utter the word of disbelief, and the tongue does not disobey him in this world. Why? Because his parts are subject to his will in the life of this world. But that disbeliever will come on the Day of Resurrection, and his parts will be removed from his will, so his parts are freed, not compelled to do deeds they do not approve of, and the parts rebel against their owner and testify against him. Someone may say: "But it is the parts that are tormented." Yes, but they accept the torment as expiation for what they did.

Thus companionship begins from the parts to the Fire: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ So if we see disbelievers doing good in this world, let each of us beware for his own self, saying: "Beware, O self, of being deceived by that good." Why? Because the disbeliever lives in the disbelief of the summit, and every deed with the disbelief of the summit is a deed that is nullified before Allah, even if it is not nullified before people.

And then Allah, exalted is He, speaks of these disbelievers: ﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it...﴾

Allah describes what these disbelievers spend during their worldly life while they are far from the way of Allah. He, glorified is He, compares it to a wind in which there is *sirr*, meaning severity. The root *ṣ-r-r* indicates severity, a loud noise, and clamor. An example of this is what Allah said about the wife of Ibrahim:

﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry, and she struck her face and said, "An old barren woman!"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 29]

She came with clamor, because she was old and barren, and it was ordinarily impossible for her to bear a child. Similarly, Allah says:

﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a screaming, violent wind﴾ [al-Haqqah: 6]

The *rih ṣarṣar* (screaming wind) is the wind that carries frost, and it has an audible sound.

As for His words ﴿like a wind in which there is sirr﴾, it means that the wind made the cold widespread and severe. Cold may exist in an area where there is no wind, and it remains in that area. But when the wind comes, it carries this cold from one place to another, so the scope of the harm it causes expands. And what does a wind with severe cold do? It causes calamities. Allah says of it: ﴿It strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it.﴾ When we hear the word *ḥarth* (tilth), we know it means the crops. Allah called it *ḥarth* so that a person would know that if he does not plough, he will not reap. Allah says:

﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the grower? If We willed, We could make it into debris, and you would be left in wonder﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 63–65]

It is as if the violent wind corrupts the tilth, which is the process necessary for growth. Ploughing (*ḥarth*) is the stirring of the earth, meaning making the soil loose so that the small roots can grow in it, become strong enough to penetrate it, and take nourishment from it. Through the loosening of ploughed soil, these roots are also able to take in the air needed for growth.

Allah, glorified is He, wants to present us with a parable (*mathal*, a comparison that makes an abstract matter concrete) about a group who are not believers and who spent their wealth in good causes, but this does not benefit them and has no use. This is in confirmation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿like the example of a wind in which there is sirr that strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾. Thus is the outcome of spending with an unbelieving intention, like the state of a field over which a wind has blown, carrying a fierce sound accompanied by cold. The word *ṣirr* contains severity, coldness, and violence. Hatim al-Ta'i, the generous of the Arabs, says to his servant: "Kindle the fire, for the night is a night of cold, and the wind, O boy, is a wind of *ṣirr*,

So that the passer-by may see your fire. If I bring a guest, you are free."

This generous man frees the slave if he guides a guest to the home of Hatim al-Ta'i. "The *layl qarr*" is the very cold night. "The *rih ṣirr*" is the severe wind accompanied by cold. We know in our own land that frost falls on some crops and destroys them. We also note here that Allah, exalted is He, brought this noble verse after He had already explained in the preceding verse that those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will avail them nothing against Allah, and their destination is the Fire. He, glorified is He, removes any doubt that may arise in the listener's mind, namely that the wealth spent by the disbelievers on good works will avail them nothing in the Hereafter, because they do not possess it.

Why?

Because an action is only performed for the reward upon it, and intention is always what determines the goal of every movement. Was it in the intention of the disbelievers, when they spent their wealth on the good that people know of, such as aid, relieving distress, and building hospitals, was it in the minds of these disbelievers that the Lord of these blessings exists? Or were they doing these things out of desire for worldly status, the praise of history, and the remembrance of humanity?

There is no doubt that they were doing them for status, or for history, or for humanity, because they do not believe in anything beyond that. They do not believe in the existence of a God, nor in the existence of another day on which they will be held to account for what they have done. We said before that whoever does a deed should seek its reward from the one for whom he did it. Since they did their deeds for this world, its remembrance, its status, and its pride, the world has given them everything.

Allah, exalted and glorified is He, presents us with a parable, and He is the One who presents parables to people so that they may remember. The meaning of a parable is that it addresses a matter of meaning which may be beyond the understanding of some minds, so it gives it a form and represents it through a sensory matter that everyone knows. We know that sensory things are the basis of abstract matters in understanding. We know that when a child's perceptions first open, he perceives the sensible thing first, and then from sensible things he forms intelligible concepts.

For example, a child sees fire, touches it, and it burns him, so the child becomes convinced that fire burns. A child drinks honey and finds it sweet, so he becomes convinced that honey has a sweet taste. A child eats something bitter like colocynth, and a known fact forms in him: that this thing has a bitter taste. Thus every piece of knowledge a person acquires through his various means of perception comes first from sensible matters.

And sensible matters, as we have learned, have as their means the five outward senses: the eye to see, the ear to hear, the nose to smell, the tongue to taste, and the fingertips to touch. Thus we know that each outward sense has a purpose in perception. A person also possesses other senses whose effects we perceive, although we do not perceive their organs or instruments.

For example: the sense of distance, by which a person knows whether the thing he sees is near him or far from him. Likewise the sense of weight, by which a person carries a thing and knows its heaviness. He perceives that heaviness through a sense other than the five outward senses. This sense is the sense of weight, by which a person discovers that one thing is heavier than another, because the muscles that carry an object know the amount of effort exerted in lifting it. There is also another, non-apparent sense, the sense of *bayn* (separation/thickness), by which a person holds cloth between his fingertips to know whether the thickness of this cloth is greater than the thickness of another cloth. To know the thickness of a thing, it must be situated between two touching surfaces.

So there are many senses that nurture meanings in us; all perceptions are the offspring of sense. For this reason Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers knowing nothing, and He made for you hearing, sight, and hearts, that you might be grateful﴾ [an-Nahl: 78]

These are the means of perception. He mentioned hearing and sight first because they are the two basic means, and after them He mentioned the *af'idah* (hearts), which are concerned with meanings, emotions, and other inner matters. So when Allah wants to give a parable about an abstract matter over which minds may differ, He brings a sensory matter upon which the senses agree. We know that in language there is a device called *tashbih* (simile). When a person does not know something, he says to his teacher: "Liken to me the thing I do not know to a thing I know." A person may ask his companion: "Do you know so-and-so?" The companion says: "I do not know him," so the person says to his companion: "So-and-so, whom you do not know, is equal to so-and-so in height, and equal to so-and-so in colour." Thus a person moves from a matter he does not know to a matter he knows. Allah, exalted is He, presents us with parables from sensory matters so that we may understand abstract matters. Allah also makes clear to us that when those who disbelieve have many gods, their faculties become disturbed. He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Allah presents an example: a man in whom are partners disputing with one another, and a man belonging entirely to one man. Are they equal in comparison? All praise is due to Allah; but most of them do not know﴾ [az-Zumar: 29]

He, glorified is He, makes clear through a plain parable the condition of a man owned by several partners. The partners who own this slave are not in agreement; rather there is dispute and discord among them. Naturally this slave must be burdened. Thus is the matter of associating partners with Allah: the slave in such a state is scattered and divided in spirit among those who own him, who are at odds with one another. As for the matter of monotheism, Allah compares it to His saying: ﴿and a man belonging entirely to one man﴾.

Thus Allah, out of mercy towards us, moves us from a lofty doctrinal meaning to a sensory meaning that everyone shares, so that we see that a man owned by one master receives his orders from one person only. Likewise, in this verse Allah wants to present a parable for one who spends something without the intention of pleasing Allah through obedience: however much this person spends, his spending is void. When we read the parables of the Noble Qur'an, we must not take only one detail. No, we must take the whole comparison so that we understand the entire parable as one composed picture, just as Allah gave us the parable of the disputing partners who own one man. Therefore we must not take the parable literally, but take the matter as a whole from the entirety of the parable. Another example: Allah, exalted is He, says:

﴿And present to them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, and then it becomes dry remnants which the winds scatter. And Allah is ever Able over all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]

Is the worldly life like water? No, but the story of the whole of life resembles the story which Allah gives as a parable. Water, when it descends, mixes with the earth, and afterwards the earth stirs and produces vegetation, and the vegetation produces beautiful flowers, and afterwards it ends as dry debris. So is this world in its adornment: the beginning is flowering, full of freshness, greenness, and joy, and the end is painful and destructive.

Thus Allah, exalted is He, conveys to us the meaning of the worldly life and likens it to flowers and plants, whose end is to become dry debris scattered by the winds. This is what He says in another place in the Noble Qur'an:

﴿So We made it [like] reaped stubble, as though it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought﴾ [Yunus: 24]

When we reflect deeply on His saying, the Truth:

﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys it. And Allah did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117]

we find in this verse a *mushabbah* (the thing being likened) and a *mushabbah bihi* (the thing likened to). The *mushabbah* is the people who spend their wealth without the intention of Allah, that is, disbelievers in Allah. The *mushabbah bihi* is the crop struck by a wind containing severe cold. The result is that there is no benefit here, nor there.

Why does the wind strike the tilth of a people who wronged themselves? Does the wind not strike the tilth of a people who did not wrong themselves?

Those who wronged themselves are struck by this calamity as a punishment, like the people of the garden about whom Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, We have tried them as We tried the companions of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning, without making any exception. Then there came upon it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep. So it became as if reaped﴾ [al-Qalam: 17–20]

Allah recompensed them for their wrongdoing. But do we not see a man who did not wrong himself, whose crop is struck by a calamity? We see this in life. A man who did not wrong himself, whose crop is struck by calamity, and who endures his calamity patiently, receives recompense and reward from Allah. Perhaps Allah has destroyed through it wealth that heedlessness had brought into his possession by an unlawful means.

Thus is the calamity for the mu-

The Lord says next: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than your own, who will not spare you [any] ruin. They wish you would have hardship...﴾

When Allah addresses the believers and calls them with His words ﴿O you who have believed﴾, know that what comes after it is a religious obligation (taklif) from the Truth, may He be glorified. So whenever the Truth calls the believers in Him, He calls them in order to impose an obligation, and He, glory be to Him, imposes obligations only on those who believe in Him. As for when He calls the one who does not believe in Him to the expanse of faith, He stirs in him the capacity to think, and says to him:

Reflect on the heavens, reflect on the earth, reflect on the phenomena of the universe, until you believe that the universe has one God. Once a person believes in the one God, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says to him: since you have believed in the one God, then receive the judgment from God.

When the Truth says ﴿O you who have believed﴾, He, glory be to Him, addresses with obligation those who believe in Him, and He imposes no command of "do" and "do not" except on those who believe. As for the one who has not believed, Allah calls him to enter the fold of faith: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾. Then when a person enters the fold of faith, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, honours this believer with obligation through "do" and "do not". And as long as the servant has believed in the capable, wise, creating, self-subsisting God, let him hear from God what will set right his life. Sometimes there occurs what outwardly suggests that Allah calls one who already believes in Him and then commands him to believe, like the saying of the Truth: ﴿O you who have believed﴾.

A person may ask how God calls one who believes in Him and then commands him to believe. Here we see that what is required of every believer is to perform the acts of faith continually and to add to them, so that the caravan of faith keeps going strong. When the Truth asks the believer for something already present in him, we should know that Allah wants from the believer the perpetuation of this kind of conduct which Allah loves. It is as if the Truth, when He says ﴿O you who have believed﴾, is carrying in this noble saying a command to persist in faith, because human beings are changeable. We know that Allah has given room for choice to people who believed and then apostatized. So the matter is not merely the declaration of faith and then the question is over; no, what is required is the persistence of faith.

When we read the saying of the Truth ﴿O you who have believed﴾, let us understand that there is a new obligation, and since there is obligation, the element of choice is present. Therefore the ground (ḥaythiyya) of every obligatory ruling from God has as its premise: ﴿O you who have believed﴾. Do not, O believer, search for the cause (ʿilla) of the ruling and ask: why have You obligated me, my Lord, with this command? It is not your right, O believer, to ask "why", since you have believed; for the Truth, glory be to Him, has imposed obligation only on those who believe in Him. So if you, O believer, have believed that He is a truthful, capable, wise God, then entrust yourself to Allah and carry out what Allah requires with "do" and "do not", whether you understand the cause or not.

We have already given an example and we continue to repeat it.

A patient who complains of indigestion after eating thinks that his digestive system has a fault, and he thinks about choosing a treating physician, and chooses a doctor specialised in the digestive system, and goes to that doctor. Here the work of the mind ends for the patient; he has chosen a doctor and decided to go to him. The doctor conducts a careful examination, requests the necessary tests if the matter requires, diagnoses the illness, then writes the medicine. And when the doctor writes the medicine for the patient, the patient may not say to the doctor: I will not take this medicine unless you convince me of its wisdom. Rather, he must carry out the doctor's words, and thus the patient obeys the doctor, though both are equal in humanity. So how should a person's courtesy be with his Creator? The whole work of the mind for the believer is to believe in God; and after you, O believer, have believed in God as wise, receive the judgment from God, because He is trusted to direct you, since you are His handiwork.

The Truth commands the believer to pray, and the believer must perform it, and does not search for the cause of prayer as if it were mere exercise, no. The command to pray comes from the Truth; and when you pray, you notice that your soul has been opened by prayer and you feel at ease, and you say to yourself: how sweet is the comfort of faith; this is the cause of the believing ruling. The cause of a believing ruling is known by the believer after he carries it out, and for this reason we find that the Truth, out of the bounty of His generosity, says to us:

﴿And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]

So when you fear Allah regarding the ruling, He gives you the cause and gives you the comfort of faith. You, O servant, do not first ask for conviction about the cause before you carry out a ruling of God, because the Truth, glory be to Him, may delay some grounds of the rulings from His creatures for long centuries. An example is that we did not know the cause of a ruling for fourteen centuries, such as the prohibition of eating pork. Should the believing servants have postponed eating pork for fourteen centuries until they had laboratories for analysis, so that we might know the harms in it—harms established through laboratory testing? No.

The believing servants did not postpone carrying out the ruling; they carried it out, and the grandchildren of grandchildren discovered that there was harm in it. This should move us to carry out every ruling whose cause we do not know. This ruling has a wisdom with God which human reason may not be able to grasp, but things will come that clarify some rulings in what a person did not know, and those clarifications give us confidence in every ruling whose cause we do not know, and the cause of every ruling becomes: ﴿O you who have believed﴾.

By this saying the Truth calls every one of His servants: O you who have believed in Me as God, take this obligation from Me. An example—and to God belongs the highest example—is when the doctor says: O you who have believed that I am a doctor for your illness, take this medicine and you will be healed, God willing.

When a person visits a sick man and asks him: why are you taking this medicine? The patient answers: the doctor prescribed this medicine for me. How much more, then, should we carry out God's rulings? We must carry them out because God has said them. Therefore, those who are deeply and earnestly wise differ from those who claim reason superficially; these serious wise people say: this reason is a mount that brings you to the gate of the sultan, but it does not enter with you into his presence. So reason brings you to believe in God, but it does not thrust itself into what is beyond its capacity.

In this coming obligation, the Truth, glory be to Him, says: ﴿O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾, meaning: since you have believed, you must preserve this faith by keeping away from it the incitement of Satan and the plotting of enemies. The incitement of Satan and the plotting of enemies come only through the intimate (biṭāna) who mixes with a person.

Let us understand the word biṭāna well. The biṭāna of a man are his close companions, that is, the people who accompany him, sit with him, and know his secrets. The word biṭāna is also derived from the lining of a garment (biṭānat al-thawb). When we hold any piece of clothing we find that the outer cloth is rough, and so the tailor puts a smooth lining in the rough garment and selects it likewise, because it is in contact with the body. A lining of friends enters upon people with softness, wins them over and enslaves them. For this reason we find the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, saying: "The Ansar are the undergarment (shiʿar), and the people are the outer garment (dithār)."

The shiʿār is the garment that touches the skin of the body, and the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, elevates the worth of those who received the Islamic call with affection and love. Thus we know that the word biṭāna is derived—as we have said—from the lining of the garment, because it is what joins with the body to protect it; we wear wool to give us warmth, and we place between it and the body a lining to keep away from the body the roughness of the wool. They call the lining "wilīja," that is, what enters into people's lives, and every evil in existence comes from this lining.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, though he is infallible, revealed to, and has companions such that any believing servant would aspire to take him as a model—this noble Messenger—we find some of his description in a dialogue between our master al-Husayn, may God be pleased with him, and his father our master ʿAlī, may God honour his face. Al-Husayn said:

"O my father, tell me about the gathering of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace."

ʿAlī, may God honour his face, said:

"The Messenger of God did not sit or stand except in remembrance (of God). And in the hadith: 'The Messenger of God used to remember God often.'"

Why? Because sitting and standing is the nullifying of one movement by another; whoever was standing and then sat has performed a movement which is sitting, and whoever was sitting and then stood has performed a movement which is standing. The Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, remembered God in every movement, giving thanks for the blessing of the Creator, the Mighty and Majestic. Each of us may ask himself: how many muscles does a person move in order to sit or stand?

They are great numbers of muscles that move to balance the rising or sitting of the body, numbers a person does not know.

So what made these deaf organs understand the will of the human being, so that as soon as a person tries to stand he stands, and as soon as he tries to sit he sits? When you raise your hand you do not know which muscles move to raise the hand, and that is a high administration of which the poet says: "And in you is folded the greater world."

As if the greater world has been folded and has become within you. If you wish to sleep you sleep, and if you want to rise you rise. The Truth shows you that your commands to your muscles and your control over the kingdom of your body are by God's subjection; you realise this when you look around and find that He, glory be to Him, has deprived anyone other than you of the ability to raise the arm. Beware of thinking that movement came to you merely because you have a hand; no, another may have a hand but cannot command it so that it moves. Thus we know that all the faculties in the soul move only by the Truth's subjecting them to serve the human being.

The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "When one of you wakes, let him say: Praise be to God who returned my soul to me, granted me health in my body, and permitted me to remember Him."

He directs the human being to remember his Creator at every standing or sitting, and our Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, teaches us that at every stirring, with every movement, we must remember the One who created us and created in us the capacity for movement.

Let each of us ask himself: how many movements does a command requiring a person to scratch his back, for example, require? It is an unknown number of movements. Thus we must show good manners toward God by remembering Him in every movement, for He is the One who created each of us fit for all these capacities.

We return to the description by ʿAlī, may God honour his face, of the gathering of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: he would not sit or stand except in remembrance.

Let us be mindful of the Messenger's precision in dealing with human intimates. Here the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, did not assign places (yuwaṭṭin al-amākin) and forbade assigning them. To assign a place (tawṭīn) means to designate a place for a particular person to sit in. The Messenger would sit wherever the gathering ended for him, and his companions likewise; no one would always sit beside him, lest someone take from his standing with the Messenger an opportunity by which others imagine he has special favour. All of them were equal. In our own age we see that some take for themselves a place in the mosque, and this is forbidden. On the authority of Ibn ʿAmr, may God be pleased with them both, he said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, forbade the pecking of the crow, the spreading of the beast, and that a man should assign a place in the mosque as a camel assigns its place."

ʿAlī, may God honour his face, adds in describing the Messenger's gathering: "When he went to a people he sat wherever the gathering ended for him, and he would sit on the ground and eat on the ground, tie the sheep's legs, and accept the invitation of a slave."

Is there any courtesy greater than this? It is the noble Messenger, sitting wherever the gathering ends for him. He...

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 119:

﴿Here you are, you love them, but they do not love you, though you believe in the whole Book. When they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage. Say: "Die in your rage. Indeed, Allah knows well what is in the breasts."﴾

The discussion of the inner circle (bitanah) continues, and it indicates that the inner circle was unable to turn the believers away from faith. Rather, the believers who had tasted the sweetness of faith tried to change the disbelievers. The disbelievers did not succeed in changing the believers, and likewise the disbelievers also failed to control themselves, and there was nothing left for these disbelievers but hypocrisy; therefore they said, "We believe." The verse shows us that the believers had understood the verses of truth. Why, then, did the Truth come with His saying, "You love them, but they do not love you"?

The believers loved the disbelievers when they explained to them the matter of truth in the methodology of Islam, and the believers wanted to spare the disbelievers the hardships of disbelief in this world and the next. This is true love. Did the disbelievers then reciprocate the love? No, because these disbelievers wanted to take the believers back to disbelief, and this is evidence of the absence of affection. The disbelievers did not manage to achieve this aim, and therefore they said, "We believe." The meaning of their saying, "We believe," shows us that the stance of the Muslims was a firm and strong stance; therefore the disbelievers found no way but to be hypocrites. ﴿And when they meet you, they say, "We believe."﴾ They said this despite the hatred visible in their mouths, and their conduct did not match what they said. Here the Muslims began to restrain and reduce their affection for the disbelievers; therefore the people of disbelief said: If this situation continues, these Muslims will surely abandon us... And so that they might avoid this situation, they professed faith outwardly, and their stance would change when they were alone with themselves. The Truth depicts this stance in His saying: ﴿But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage.﴾ So what is the biting?

Linguistically, biting ('add) is the meeting of the two jaws upon something in order to crush it. And what are the anamil? They are the tips of the fingers. The anamil have a certain delicacy and a certain lightness of movement, derived from the nimble movement of the ant (khaliyat al-naml). They are also called al-banan. When we observe the act of biting the fingertips, we find it to be an involuntary, compulsive emotional act. That is, the intellect does not arrange it; no one is pleased to continue committing the act of biting his own fingers, for biting a finger causes pain. But being filled with rage drives a person to bite his fingers as a compulsive matter resulting from disturbance and imbalance in emotion.

And from where does the rage come?

Rage came upon the disbelievers because they were unable to shift the believers by a single hair from the path of God. Rather, the opposite happened: the believers tried to draw the disbelievers toward the light of faith, while the disbelievers wanted to make themselves an inner circle through which they could enter among the believers to spread their corruption. Therefore they fell into rage when the believers did not allow them any of their aims.

A person sometimes falls prey to rage when he cannot declare his anger toward his adversary. For this reason, if a believer wants to confront the envy of one of his opponents, he must increase his virtue over that person, and then this opponent grows in rage and bitterness. Also, we find that among the teachings of Islam is that the believer does not repay an evil done to him by another with evil, so that he does not commit the same sin; rather he follows the well-known saying:

"We do not repay one who disobeys God regarding us with anything more than obeying God regarding him."

When the Muslims treat them well, they increase in enmity, rage and hatred toward Islam. The early Muslims behaved in this manner; they were firm mountains of faith.

The enemies of Islam disobey God through their bad treatment of the Muslims, but the Muslims answer bad treatment with good treatment. When the enemies of Islam see that their scheming does not achieve its goal, they fall into the well and the mire of rage. When the disbelievers are alone with themselves, their first act is to bite their fingers from rage, and this, as I have explained, is the result of compulsive emotion following anger and inability to achieve the aim; for every perceptual impact on the human soul knocks at an emotional domain within it.

The emotional domain must express itself through a conative process that appears in movement. When a person causes someone he knows some form of anger, he becomes agitated quickly and erupts in words; this is evidence of the good nature of the angry person. As for the one who does not show his emotion, he must be guarded against, for he stores up his emotions and controls them, so one does not know when they will appear or in what form they will show. For this reason the saying says: "Beware the rage of the forbearing one." When new emotions gather upon old accumulated emotions in the heart of the forbearing one, no one knows when the measure will overflow.

Thus perception gives rise to emotion, and the person is moved by a conative, kinetic impulse. The Islamic legislation does not want a person to be a deaf stone that feels nothing, but it asks the Muslim to be moved by a refined emotion. Therefore the Truth sets out a method for the believer, and He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Those who restrain their anger and pardon people; and Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]

The Qur'an acknowledges that there are events that call forth a person's anger, and the one who never gets angry at all is following a path that does not accord with the sound nature of human beings. God wants a person to be a human being, with his feelings, sentiments and emotions, but God, the true Educator, refines the emotions of this person. For us, the Prophet (ﷺ) is a good example. When his son Ibrahim died:

He (ﷺ) said: "The eye weeps and the heart grieves, and we say only what pleases our Lord. And indeed, O Ibrahim, we are saddened by your parting."

The Prophet (ﷺ) combined emotion with faith. The eye weeps, the heart grieves, and a person is not deaf in the face of events; rather, a person must be emotionally moved in a refined way.

When the Qur'an describes the sound human being, it does not place the believer in an iron mold so that he cannot change, and so He, glorified is He, says:

﴿Humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]

Thus the believer is not made innately humble, nor innately mighty; rather he responds to different situations. This situation calls for humility and modesty toward the believers, so the believer is humble; and there is another situation that calls for might against arrogant disbelievers, so the believer is mighty. The Truth, glorified is He, says of the believers:

﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His good pleasure.﴾ [al-Fath: 29]

Mercy is not a fixed trait, nor is severity a fixed trait; rather the believers respond to events. When the believer is with the believers, he is merciful; when he confronts the disbelievers, he is strong and severe. God, glorified is He, does not want the believer to be in one rigid mold, so the Truth says:

﴿Those who restrain their anger and pardon people; and Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]

And He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished.﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]

Thus the Truth did not prevent the believer from punishing someone for a wrong, because He created creation and knows them well, and it is not possible for Him to contradict their nature, and so that the believer will not be threatened in his faith later on; for if the believer abandons his rights, the disbelievers will rage and roam through the rights of the Muslims. For this reason the believer trains himself to inflict punishment even upon a believer who errs, so that the believer knows how to punish any transgressor against a right of God's rights. The believer is also required to elevate his punishment: he either punishes with the like of what he was punished with, or he rises higher, and listens to the saying of the Truth:

﴿But if you are patient, it is better for the patient.﴾ [al-Nahl: 126]

The Truth has set out the method of elevation after giving the believer the right to inflict retaliatory punishment. Thus God has not forced the nature of man; and had He wished that, He would not have created this nature. He, glorified is He, makes clear to us that there is an emotion of rage, and that the believer must try to restrain his rage, that is, not express his rage in a conative way. If the believer removes this matter from his heart, it means that he has become healed of it and has risen.

Thus restraining rage means that the believer does not express his rage in a conative way. If someone reviles you, you do not revile him. This restraint means suppressing the emotion in the heart. If the believer rises further and ignores even the emotion itself, he removes the rage from his heart, and by this he rises to a higher level. The Truth describes this as entering the rank of ihsan (excellence), for He says: ﴿and Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ Thus the believer treats well the one who caused his rage with a good word.

As for the one who caused your rage, O believer, when you have restrained your rage in the first stage and pardoned in the second stage, and removed the emotion from your heart, you reach the third stage, which represents the peak of faith: it is ihsan... ﴿and Allah loves the good-doers.﴾ The one who caused the rage must reflect upon himself and regret what he did.

Islam did not ignore human feelings when it demanded that believers treat well those who wrong them. Whoever looks carefully and understands precisely knows that Islam granted the believer the right in human nature when He said: ﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished,﴾ but it elevated the believer.

When we look at this matter as an economic question, reckoning it in terms of "what is his" and "what is for him," we find that the believer has gained. An example of this — and to God belongs the highest likeness — is when a father finds one of his sons has wronged a brother of his; the father's heart is with the wronged one. Suppose a person wronged a servant of God; then God, as a Lord who educates, is jealous for him. We know that someone said to a knower of God:

"Do you show kindness to one who wronged you?" The knower of God said: "Should I not show kindness to one whom God has placed at my side?"

Now let us return to the rage of the disbelievers against the believers. The rage of the disbeliever arises because his believing opponent wishes him faith and bears no grudge in his heart, while the disbeliever seethes with hatred, and because of this he nearly loses his composure; therefore the Truth says: ﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage.﴾

As for "alone," it means that when the disbelievers find themselves in a disbelieving society with no Muslim among them, they declare their rage at the believers. They did this act, biting the fingertips out of rage, in the absence of faith and of the believers in God. If these disbelievers had any sense at all, would they not have reflected on how the Qur'an exposed them, they who committed this act far from the believers?

Would their thinking not have led them to realize that there is a Lord of the believers who discloses the hidden matters to His Messenger, and the Messenger conveys them to the believers?

Yet they still did not understand this exposure of them: ﴿And when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you out of rage.﴾ Here we must understand that there is a matter that may cause rage, but a person may be too timid to vent his anger. If someone angers you, you may go to him and react against him, or you may react against yourself, and this is what is called "diversion of the impulse." The angry person is filled with angry energy, and the one he is angry at may be strong and influential, so he fears to react against him...

And after that He says, may He be exalted: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all...﴾

The Qur'an is the speech of God, and to Him, glory be to Him, belongs complete eloquence and perfect richness. Expressions conveying one and the same meaning may differ, because every context has its own wording, and He, glory be to Him, determines with extreme precision the word that fits. It is He, glory be to Him, who said:

﴿Indeed, man was created anxious. When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding; except for those who pray, who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19-23]

And He, the Exalted, said:

﴿Whatever good reaches you is from God, and whatever evil reaches you is from yourself. And We sent you to mankind as a messenger, and sufficient is God as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 79]

He, may He be exalted, speaks of "touching" (mass) with regard to evil and good, and at other times speaks of what happens to a person as "striking" (isabah) with good or evil. In the verse we are reflecting upon, you find a difference in style: He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it﴾. He did not present the whole matter as "touching," nor did He present it entirely as "striking." This is the speech of a Wise Lord, and when we reflect on its meaning, one of us says: this is a speech that none but a Wise Lord would utter.

Now let us become acquainted with "mass" (mass) and "striking" (isabah). Some scholars said: mass and isabah have one meaning, based on His, the Truth's, saying:

﴿Indeed, man was created anxious. When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 19-21]

But we say that mass is the establishing of a connection between the toucher and the touched. If a man touches his wife, we command him only to perform wudu', because the mere contact of the toucher with the touched, which does not bring about major impurity (janabah), requires no ghusl. Striking (isabah), however, is contact plus something more: one who slaps a person may swell his temple, for the palm meets the cheek and strikes the temple. Thus we know that there is a difference between mass and isabah. When the Truth says: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them﴾...

This means that the good that reaches them is slight, not great; it is merely a spoil or a little good. In our daily lives we find someone filled with rage because his rival has gained ten piastres, and someone may say to him: why do you not save your rage until he gains a hundred pounds, for example? Such rage over a small good is a sign that every good that comes to the believers causes weariness and distress to the disbelievers. Merely the touch of good upon the believers wearies the disbelievers, so what of when evil befalls them?

The Truth says: ﴿But if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it﴾. The disbelievers rejoice at any harm that befalls the believers, even though human nature would require that the envier turn into one who shows mercy: "Let it suffice you from an incident befalling a man that you see his envious ones showing mercy to him."

That is, let it suffice you from an incident or calamity befalling a person that the one who used to envy him turns into one who shows mercy to him and says: "By God, I am saddened on his account."

So when the believers' affliction intensifies, does that change the disbelievers' stance? No. The people of disbelief used to rejoice at the people of faith, and when any good comes to the believers, they grieve. The Truth says: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them﴾, and "good" is any good that touches them lightly. ﴿But if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all﴾. So however much they scheme against you, they will not harm you in any way.

What is required of you is to be patient in the face of their enmity, patient in the face of their evil, patient in the face of their joy at calamities, and patient in the face of their grief over a blessing that reaches you or touches you. Be patient, and you will have immunity; their scheming will not reach you. Be patient and fear God, so that you may ensure that God is on your side: ﴿If you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all﴾.

And what is scheming (kayd)? Scheming is that you plot and devise to inflict harm upon another in such a way that it appears to come from someone other than you; that is, you plan against another in order to harm him. The root of kayd is taken from kayd and kabad, which have one meaning, for what afflicts the liver (kabid) causes pain, because the kabid is the strong piece of flesh in a person; when something strikes it, it wearies and incapacitates a person. They say: so-and-so struck the kabid of the truth, meaning he reached the point of strength in the matter he is describing.

And what is the meaning of yubayyitun? They said: scheming by night (tabyit) is not a sign of courage, and whenever you see someone plotting and deceiving, know that he is a coward, for the brave one does not scheme or deceive; rather, it is the weak one who cannot face others who schemes and deceives. So if you are patient in the face of the requirements of their enmity and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all, because God will be with you.

The Truth concludes the verse with the noble statement: ﴿Indeed, God is encompassing of what they do﴾. Whenever you see the word "muhit" (encompassing), it indicates to you that He knows everything. And ihatah (encompassing) means that not a single need escapes Him. Here is a real experience in the history of Islam, in which the Truth affirms with emphasis: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed, God is encompassing of what they do﴾. Each of us should remember the truth of this matter.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 3, verse 121:

﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for the fighting; and Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾

In this instance, at the battle of Uhud, the disbelievers came with three thousand men, while the Muslims were few, only seven hundred fighters. In order to make clear the truth of His promise in His words: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all﴾, the intended meaning here is not secret plotting (al-kayd al-tabyeeti) but their open action. That is, remember the truth of this matter:

﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family﴾. The ghadwah (ghadwa) is the early part of the day, and the rawah (rawah) is the late part of the day. The word "ahl" (family) may be used to mean a wife, and what is intended here is the room of 'A'ishah, for the Messenger was in it at this time, the time when the disbelievers of Quraysh wished to avenge themselves for their dead and their captives from Badr. They gathered their hosts, for every aggrieved party from the battle of Badr had horsemen and men. So much so that after the battle of Badr, their leader Abu Sufyan said to his companions: "Tell the women not to weep for your dead, for weeping removes grief." Tears are called "washing away of sorrow" or "melting of longing." When a grieving person weeps, those around him say: "Leave him to rest."

Had the women grieved and wept over the dead of Badr, the flame of vengeance would have subsided. Therefore Abu Sufyan said: "Tell them not to weep." He wanted the rage over the matter of Badr to remain present until they had taken revenge. Indeed, the camp of unbelief gathered three thousand fighters at Uhud. After that, the Prophet (ﷺ) consulted his companions on this matter, and he sent for one of the greatest hypocrites, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and he did not summon him except for this battle. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and most of the Ansar said:

"O Messenger of Allah, we have never gone out to an enemy outside Madinah without being harmed by them, and no enemy has entered upon us without our inflicting harm upon them. We see that you should not go out to them. If they remain, they remain in a wretched confinement; if they enter it, the men will fight them face to face, and the women and children will pelt them with stones from above; and if they return, they will return disappointed." Others among the Companions urged going out to them, and they said:

"O Messenger of Allah, lead us out against our enemies, so that they do not see that we have shrunk from them and grown weak." The proponents of this view did not cease urging the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he agreed to what they wanted.

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered his house, put on his armour and took up his weapons. Those who had insisted on his going out thought that they had compelled him to what he did not want, and they regretted what they had done. When he came out to them, they said: "We forced you, O Messenger of Allah, and that was not for us to do. If you wish, remain seated." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "It is not fitting for a Prophet who has put on his armour to take it off until he fights."

They went out to war, and this is what the Qur'an reminds of, confirming the matter mentioned in the preceding verse: ﴿And if you are patient and mindful of Allah, their plotting will not harm you at all. Indeed, Allah is encompassing of what they do.﴾

Mention, O Muhammad:

﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for the fighting﴾ [Al 'Imran: 121]

And ﴿tubawwi'u al-mu'minina maqa'ida lil-qital﴾ means: to settle the believers in places for fighting. One says "bawwa'tu fulanan," meaning: I settled him in a place to which he returns (yabu'u ilayhi, i.e., returns), and its name is "watan" (homeland), because a person returns to his homeland.

Observe the precision of expression in the Word of the Truth: ﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family, you station the believers at their positions for the fighting﴾, that is, you make for them a dwelling-place and a homeland. The word "maqa'id" means places of steadfastness, and war is advance, retreat and standing firm; the one who fights is made firm by Allah in the battle, so it is as if he is settled in the field. Thus the Messenger's command to the fighters implies that none of them should turn to any other place than the position in which he was made firm and settled, meaning: this is now your homeland, because your faithful destiny will depend upon it.

So His words: ﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family, you station﴾ mean: you settle "the believers," and you say to them: your homeland is your positions in which you have been made firm. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought the archers and appointed over them "Abdullah ibn Jubayr," and they were fifty men that day. The Messenger said to them: "Stand fast in your ranks here, and protect our backs. If you see us winning, do not join us; and if you see us being killed, do not come to our aid."

But they were unable to hold to this, because their souls inclined toward the spoils. Allah willed that the test take place in the presence of His Messenger (ﷺ), so as to show the believers, in all the battles that would follow, that obeying the commander's order must be the foundation of soldiership. If you oppose the Messenger, you will inevitably be defeated.

Someone may say: Islam was defeated at Uhud. We say: No, Islam was victorious. Had the Muslims been victorious at Uhud despite the archers' disobedience of the Prophet's command, would the Messenger's command have been upheld?

So those Muslims who did not carry out the order were defeated, and it was necessary that they experience this while they were with the Messenger (ﷺ). When the wind of victory blew upon the believers at the start of the battle, the fighters began to occupy themselves with spoils and booty. The archers said: "The spoils will be taken by others, and they will leave us," and they descended to take the booty. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who was then on the religion of his people, seized the opportunity, encircled them, and what happened, happened. The news spread among the people that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been killed, and they turned back and fled. The Messenger began calling out: "To me, servants of Allah!" until a group of his Companions gathered around him, and he rebuked them for their flight. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we ransom you with our fathers and mothers. News reached us of your death, our hearts were terrified, and we turned back in flight."

Historical investigation of the battle of Uhud has confirmed that the matter cannot be considered either a defeat or a victory, because the battle was still in flux.

Afterward, the Messenger summoned those who had been with him at the battle of Uhud to go out in pursuit of the enemy, and they overtook them at Hamra' al-Asad, and the disbelievers fled. Indeed, Allah willed to give the believers a lesson in adhering to the Messenger's command (ﷺ), and the Truth said: ﴿And [remember] when you set out early from your family to station the believers at their positions for the fighting﴾.

The Truth reminds of the responsibilities of the commander, who distributes the tasks: this is the right wing and that is the left wing, this is the vanguard and this is the rearguard. The Truth concludes this with His words: ﴿And Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾, so that the believers know that He, glorified is He, has witnessed that His Messenger settled the believers at their positions for the fighting; and He, glorified is He, is "Knowing" of what occurs in intentions, because in war the matter is a defense of faith, not the submission of molds, but the submission of hearts before the submission of molds.

The Lord says after that: ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally...﴾

Al-fashal (فشل) is cowardice (al-jubn). The two groups were Banu Harithah from the Aws, and Banu Salamah from the Khazraj. These were the right wing and the left wing. They came along the way to the battle and heard the words of the hypocrite Ibn Salul, when he said to them: "There will be no fighting, because as soon as the fighters of Quraysh see us, they will flee."

The hypocrite Ibn Salul also said to the Messenger: "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." But Abdullah ibn Harithah said: "I implore you by Allah, I implore you by the Messenger of Allah, I implore you by your religion." So they went on to the fighting and stood firm after they had resolved to turn back.

What is meant here by al-hamm (الهم, resolve or intention)? Al-hamm is the stirring of a thought toward some action. This thought, in a second stage, becomes a determination and a resolve. Thus what happened from them was merely a thought of withdrawal, but they stood firm.

Why is that? Allah intended by this to show that Islam is realistic in its view of the human being, for a person has many passing thoughts. Therefore the Truth (al-Haqq) raises this matter to give us the remedy. So He said: ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾.

One of the two groups said: "By Allah, I would not be pleased that I had not resolved" — that is, his heart was relieved because he had resolved — "because I am assured of being among those about whom Allah said: ﴿and Allah is their ally﴾, and the wilayah (guardianship) of Allah is sufficient for me." He rejoiced because he had received the decoration, which is the wilayah of Allah.

Thus we draw inspiring lessons from these noble verses about the Battle of Uhud. We know that this battle followed the Battle of Badr al-Kubra. The Battle of Badr al-Kubra ended in victory for the Muslims, although they were few in number and equipment. At Badr the Muslims did not go out to the battle to fight a war, but to seize the wealth of Quraysh in the caravan, as compensation for their property that they had left behind in Makkah. Yet Allah willed that they not confront the loaded caravan, but that they confront the armed party (al-fi'ah dhat al-shawkah), and victory came to them.

But this victory, although it instilled awe of the Muslims in the hearts of their enemies, also gathered the resolve of the enemies of Islam to unite in order to deliver a blow by which they would restore the prestige of unbelief. That is why we saw the leaders of Quraysh forbidding their women to weep over their dead, because weeping relieves the weary soul, and they wanted the grief to remain suppressed in order to produce a vengeful fervour that would move the human soul to take revenge for these dead. This is on the side of emotion, which they wished to keep kindled. On the side of wealth, they kept the money of the caravan that had escaped, so that it would be a means of arranging a battle in which they would restore their prestige.

Before Uhud they tried to do something, but they were turned back on their heels. For example, Abu Sufyan led a force of one hundred men and wanted to attack Madinah with it. When news of it reached our master, the Messenger of Allah, he set out with his companions against them. Abu Sufyan learned of the Messenger's departure and fled, and he threw away the provisions he had with him on the road in order to lighten the load on the animals so they would move faster. That is why it is called the Ghazwat al-Sawiq (Battle of the Sawiq), because they left their food, which was sawiq (a porridge of ground grain).

Likewise some of the unbelievers tried to raid Madinah more than once after that, but the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would go out against them at the head of fighters: once their number was one hundred, once one hundred and fifty, and once two hundred. Indeed the Messenger ﷺ scattered their gathering. It was his method, when he went to a people who, he was informed, wanted to plot an attack on Madinah, to remain in their land and in their camp for a considerable time.

All of that preceded the Battle of Uhud. After that they gathered to come to the Battle of Uhud, and what happened happened. The verses that deal with this battle contain allusions to what took place in it. The Messenger ﷺ stationed the fighters in positions for battle and ordered them to remain firm in those positions. But some of the fighters left their place, and others resolved to withdraw, but then they stood firm at last, and the unbelievers of Quraysh fled. In this battle the great signs of Allah were manifested.

When Allah, glory be to Him, gave the Muslims victory at Badr, though they were few, they had not gone out for a battle but to seize a caravan. Perhaps some people thought that merely by being attributed to Allah and to Islam they would be given victory in this same manner, and would neglect the means. So Allah willed to teach them that it is necessary to exhaust the means, by preparing equipment and numbers, and by obeying the instructions of a commander.

When they disobeyed, what had to happen happened. The disobedience arose only after a beginning of victory. That is why later there will come sixty verses about this battle, to show us the criterion of the lesson in all its phases, so that we may extract from it admonition and instruction. We know that the victorious usually have ease, but the discussion here concerns the defeat of those who do not take up the means of Allah, and this is a matter that needs a pause. So the Qur'an came here to relate to us a portion of the battle, so that we may extract from it lesson and admonition. The first lesson:

When they went out, the hypocrites under the leadership of Ibn Ubayy withdrew. So the battle came to test the believers. Testing (al-tamhis) comes to the believer and rubs him thoroughly, and shows from him the measure of his steadfastness and certainty. Truly Allah tests the believing group because it will be entrusted, throughout all of history until the Hour is established, with the protection of this creed. None can bear this matter except people who have firm hearts, a strong composure in hardship, and a resolve before which all the adornments of this world are as nothing.

After that He deals with the human soul in its human conditions. The articles of faith do not settle into the hearts of Muslims merely by declaring faith, but every occasion gives a push of belief, and after that the whole matter of belief takes form. That is why the Truth shows us that two groups of believers had resolved to withdraw. They are human souls. But did the two groups carry out that resolve, or did they return and revert to the command of Allah? The two groups returned.

Thus we saw among those who had declared their faith a group that recoiled from the very beginning, and a group that went out and then returned.

The souls spoke, but the individuals of that group did not stop at the talk of the soul; they stood firm until the end. Some stood firm to the superficial aim of the matter, like the archers who saw the victory first. These were among those who stood firm; they did not flee at first with Ibn Ubayy, and they were not of the group that resolved, but they were among those who stood firm. Yet at the first glimmer of victory they longed for the spoils, and they disobeyed the Messenger's command. Let us read His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And Allah had already fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you are those who desire this world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them to test you. And He has already pardoned you, and Allah is full of bounty toward the believers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]

After that comes another point, which is not to be tempted by any human being. Khalid ibn al-Walid, the champion of the camp of unbelief at Uhud, is the one who exploited the opportunity when the archers left their positions. After that he encircled the army of the believers, and what happened, happened. As for Khalid before he embraced Islam, was he not at the Battle of the Trench? Indeed he was at the Battle of the Trench. He was also in many other campaigns with the forces of polytheism. Where, then, was his genius in those campaigns?

The genius of men contends with the genius of men, but there is no human genius able to override a divine arrangement. That is why Khalid's role did not appear in the Battle of the Trench; it appeared at the Battle of Uhud, because the opponents of Khalid disobeyed the command of their leadership. So human genius remained against human genius, but if they had remained within the embrace of the divine method of direction, Khalid's genius could never have prevailed over the arrangements of his Lord.

The historical investigation of all the military men who have studied the Battle of Uhud says: there was no defeat for the Muslims and no victory for the unbelievers, because victory requires that one party drive the other from the battlefield, and that the winning party remain on the battlefield. Did Quraysh remain on the battlefield, or did they flee? Quraysh fled.

Victory is also defined by capturing some of the opposing party. Did Quraysh capture a single Muslim? No. They knew that Madinah was empty of all the believers, and that in it there were only those hypocrites who had stayed behind, and the weak women and children, but their superficial triumph did not qualify them to enter Madinah.

So they neither took captives, nor seized booty, nor entered Madinah, nor remained on the battlefield. How, then, can you call this a victory? Let us say: the battle was inconclusive (ma'at al-ma'rakah), and the Muslims remained on the battlefield.

Here the true heroism becomes manifest, because, as we said, in the case of victory the matter is ease, and even one who did not perform well in the battle seizes the chance of victory and surges and roams about. But the defeated, and the one whose commander, the Messenger ﷺ, was wounded and weakened so that he could not climb the mountain, Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah bowed his back to the Messenger of Allah so that he could mount him and climb to the rock.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was bleeding after his front tooth (rubaiyyah) was broken, and two rings of the helmet entered his cheek. After this, what would the situation be? So much so that the rumour-mongers spread rumours and said: the Messenger of Allah has been killed.

All of this is part of the testing. Whoever stands firm in this situation is the one who is entrusted to bear arms to support the word of Allah until the Hour is established. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ looked for one of the champions of the Muslims who had been near him, but did not find him. He was Sa'd ibn al-Rabi'.

The Messenger ﷺ said: "Who will look for me what Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' has done? Is he among the living or among the dead?" A man of the Ansar, who was Ubayy ibn Ka'b, said: "I went to search for him, and I found him wounded seventy times, between sword strikes, spear thrusts, and arrow shots." When he saw him, he said to him: "The Messenger of Allah sends you his greetings, and says to you: how do you find yourself?" that is, how are you?

Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' said: "Tell the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: May Allah reward you on our behalf with the best reward any prophet has been rewarded by his nation. And tell the Ansar: there is no excuse for you before Allah if harm reaches the Messenger of Allah while there is an eye among you that blinks." Then his soul departed.

Look at his last act. When he was overwhelmed with wounds in the battle and could no longer fight with his blade, he seized the remainder of his life to fight with his speech, so that his words would resound in the ears of the Muslims. And let him know that those who inflicted wounds on him only brought him closer to the meeting with his Lord, and that he was going to Paradise. That is the goal every believer hopes for.

We also find that those whom the Qur'an excuses from attending battles volunteer for the battles! For example Amr ibn al-Jamuh, who was lame, and lameness is an excuse that Allah established along with sickness and blindness, for He, glory be to Him, is the one who says:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick.﴾ [al-Nur: 61]

Amr ibn al-Jamuh had four sons, like lions, who had gone to the battle.
